utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Registrar, kindly call the case.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Thank you and good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-03-67-PT, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much. Today is Tuesday, and I greet all the people in the courtroom, Ms. Dahl, Mr. Seselj, and all the people helping us in our work. This is a Status Conference and this is bound to be the last one before the Pre-Trial Conference which is going to take place on the 6th of November. At the last minute, I decided to convene the Status Conference on the ground that this courtroom had become free because there was a cancellation of a witness in another case. This Status Conference is going to make it possible to put an end and to finalise some issues that were still pending. Before we go into the agenda, Mr. Seselj, I want to address my condolences to you since your mother has deceased. I was told about it when you were visited by your wife, and at the time I told the Legal Officer that if you wished to apply for provisional release in order to attend the funeral of your mother, as far as I was concerned, I would be in favour of it. So this is what I wanted to convey to you. Once again, my sincere condolences for this tragic event. Let me now move to other items that have to do with the Status Conference. First of all, Mr. Seselj, only this morning I realised that on the 17th of October you had sent a document that was filed with the registry regarding the certificate provided by -- to associates of Slobodan Milosevic confirming the existence of certain suspicions regarding witnesses who testified or could have testified in the Milosevic case. And in your submissions I found this morning you explained why you were against the proceedings governed by Rule 72 -- 92 ter. I'm somewhat surprised by your arguments. I am under the impression that you do not quite understand the principle underlying this rule or the application of it. I'm going to say what I have already said because it may be that the Prosecution may wish to call witnesses under Rule 92 ter. The proceedings ruled by this provision is as follows: When a witness has provided a written statement, the Prosecutor may apply for the implementation of the 92 ter proceedings by filing a request or a motion for admission of the written statement, but also with a phase of cross-examination. As a result, the accused, therefore, you in this instant case, you can personally -- you'll find yourself in a situation when you're not prejudiced because you are entitled to cross-examine the witness as to the contents of his written statement. Moreover, through other questions you can challenge his credibility if you are of the view that the witness is not credible in the statements he made. Therefore, the Rule 92 ter proceedings do not mean that a written statement will be automatically tendered into evidence and admitted without any cross-examination. There will in any case be cross-examination. The only advantage there is in this proceeding is that we can save time because instead of having the Prosecutor asking questions, the answers of which we already find in the written statements, the Prosecutor will only ask the witness whether he would answer in the same way now as he did in the written statements. And the witness will answer yes, and that's it. So it's very fast. It's a very speedy way of proceeding because the time devoted to the Prosecution's questions is very limited. The Prosecutor will only ask the witness whether he or she would say the same thing if he or she were asked the same thing again; and secondly, whether any -- they wish any changes to be made. However, the Prosecutor can ask of the witness some specifications, some more details about answers, and can produce some documents. However, the time devoted for cross-examination which was scheduled initially does not change inasmuch as this witness is part of the 65 ter list. For instance, if the Prosecutor had planned two hours for the witness and then for some unknown reason the Prosecutor were to change the witness, there was supposed to be a viva voce witness into a 92 ter witness, then the Prosecution will not use the two hours, maybe only 20 or 25 minutes. However, that Defence will keep the two hours that had been granted to the Defence. You will keep your two hours for cross-examination. This is what I wanted to tell you because in your submissions I realised that you entertain some fears, and I do not think that they are founded because you do not quite grasp the way this rule is implemented, because it is a rule that fully guarantees your rights. You are free to cross-examine the witness, and it is only at the end of the cross-examination that at the request of the Prosecutor and further to possible objections by the Defence, that the written statement would be admitted in whole or part. Or, as the case may be, would be dismissed. Therefore, prior to the cross-examination there's no admission of the written statement under Rule 92 ter. A written statement is only admitted after cross-examination and after the Trial Chamber has heard your observations. So this is what I wanted to tell you, Mr. Seselj, on this question that has been worrying you for a long time. I can understand that you may have some fears, but these are not justified because you do have cross-examination. There's no Rule 92 ter in the absence of a witness or in the absence of cross-examination. You can have the floor if you have something to say.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I have every respect for you trying to save time during this trial, but you cannot save trial at the expense of my procedural rights. The Prosecution over these five years has saved an awful lot of time, and now it faces a deadlock. That's not my fault that they're facing a deadline. Now, in view of the fact that statements under 92 ter are not statements written by the witness but they are statements written by either the investigators or the Prosecutor, there's no reason for me or there's no sense in me cross-examining that witness. It would be better for me to cross-examine either the Prosecutor or the investigator. Here in court a mummy will appear, some mummy, some zombie, who is going to answer in the affirmative saying that the statement is his, whereas he won't have any idea of the contents of that statement. And to add to that somebody will dictate what his answers to my questions should be through his headsets and there's no sense in that. And the main reason why I'm opposed to the introduction of witnesses under Rule 92 ter and 92 quater were introduced into the Rules of Procedure and Evidence last year, and I have been here since the 24th of February, 2003. At the last Status Conference, I quoted a provision from the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court according to which procedural rights to my detriment cannot be amended retroactively, and I am going to adhere to that. Rule 92 ter and Rule 92 quater cannot, therefore, be applied in Anglo-Saxon or in continental law, that is impossible or in any dominant legal system is there any room for behaviour of that kind. But if you insist upon that, of course I don't have the possibility of preventing you, but you then have the possibility of saving a maximum amount of time because all the Prosecution witnesses can be admitted under 92 ter and 92 quater. I will refuse to cross-examine any of them, and you can get through this trial by the 15th of November or the end of November at the latest, and then that is a maximum saving of time with my cooperation because you have my full cooperation that way. I won't be cross-examining witnesses like that, and you on the basis of the statements written by the Prosecutor can bring in your own judgement. And I think for the history, the history of international criminal law, this precedent would have enormous importance and would resound and I'm sure that in the next 300 or 400 years this will be quoted in textbooks of international criminal law and in scholarly texts and scientific work. Now, since I've shown to you on the basis of the statements of associates of Mr. Slobodan Milosevic that my concerns are justified, I can tell you that the third associate Zdenko Tomanovic has promised to write a statement along those lines, although he didn't happen to be in Belgrade so he wasn't able to do that on time so that I could attach his statement along with my written submission. I hope to do that in due course subsequently. It's up to you to weigh up the matter and to decide. Whatever you decide, I shall respect your decision, but I don't have to implement it fully. I will respect it in that I will continue to take part in these proceedings, and that I will sit calmly while the witnesses file by, the witnesses under 92 ter, 92 quater can't file past the courtroom here, so we're not going to be able to establish whether they ever gave those statements; and we've had experience in other trials according to which many witnesses of that kind have absolutely no idea of what it says in their own statements. So as I say we can complete the trial very quickly and I won't do anything on my part to slow down that speedy rounding off of the trial and you can do what you like.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. Seselj, I've been listening to you carefully, and I do understand what you're saying. It is not my intention at all to admit 92 ter statements without there having been cross-examination, but I have to go down into the details of it all because you said some things that might be confusing to those who are not aware of our proceedings in this Tribunal. You said, and you are right in saying so, you said that written statements are drafted in English and signed by witnesses. And from what you say - and this is where you may not be quite right - according to you, you say that the written statements in fact reflects what the investigator would have said and not what the witness would have said. This is, I think, worthy of some of my comments. As you know, the proceedings in this Tribunal are of a mixed nature, part of common law and part of continental law. In your country, as in mine, the investigative process is controlled by a judge, which is not the case here. Here investigations are conducted solely under the control of the Prosecutor. So what happens? When there is a witness, a witness who speaks B/C/S, he or she meets with the investigator of the Office of the Prosecutor, generally investigators are former policemen hailing from various countries, and sometimes during the interview there may be a representative of the OTP who will also or sometimes ask questions. Based on that there is -- an interview, a discussion between the witness and the OTP. Such discussions may go over several days, up to ten days. It is not uncommon to see that such interviews have taken two, three, four were or five days. And following the interview which is recorded, what is going to happen? The investigator drafts a written statement, and the statement is supposed to contain all the statements made by the witness and the witness's answers to the questions put by the investigator. It may happen that it is a document with several pages, ten or less sometimes. The witness will sign the document, a document that is drafted in English. The translation into B/C/S will be done later or sometimes it is at the same time. When it is a document of several pages, the translation may eventuate later. Whatever the case may be, when the witness signs, he's supposed to know in his own language what is contained in the document because the witness has the help of an interpreter. Therefore, when the witness signs, he's supposed to be aware of the very contents of the document. The fact of saying that he has signed while investigators may have added some paragraphs to his statement, this is what seems to be contained in the submissions or in Mr. Rakic's statement is of course for surprise for me or concern because Mr. Rakic seems to suggest that witnesses in the Milosevic cases, some 12 of them, said that things had been added on to their statements by investigators. So -- well, I'm not in a position to check that because I do not have before me the written statements and the transcripts of their testimonies with cross-examination conducted by Slobodan Milosevic, but this is what Mr. Rakic is saying in his letter. In the event that this would be true, and it's only a possibility, I'm saying that conditionally, since you have the possibility of cross-examining yourself and you are in the courtroom, you have before you the written statement. Therefore, through your questions you can tell the witness, Well, you said this in paragraph 4. Is this what you stated or not? The witness will then be able to say yes or no or will be able to say that he's amazed to find that in his statement. That shows the relevance of cross-examination, since it makes it possible for you to put questions based on the written statement. And if it turns out that the witness says, No, I've never said this, it was just put into the statement by the investigator, the Trial Chamber could call the investigator to ask them for explanations because then we would be in a blatant case of perjury or forging. All this to tell you that cross-examination under 92 ter enables the accused, should they entertain doubts as to the contents of a written statement, to ask all necessary questions so that the truth can be shown. This being said, the two individuals showing some suspicions do so without thinking -- or seem to believe that some questions were prompted by the Prosecution during cross-examination were prompted to the witness following the questions put in cross-examination. Last time I told you that technically speaking this seems to be an impossible thing to be done, but these people having doubts or suspicions, this could actually arise from the proofing session. You may not know this, but I think you do. Prior to a testimony before a witness comes into the courtroom there is a habit here, custom, for what it's worth. The Prosecution can meet with the witness before the hearing takes place. Therefore, the Prosecution and the witness meet 24 hours or 48 hours before the testimony in order to prepare for the testimony. And it is likely to think that during the proofing session the Prosecutor is going to tell the witness that he's going to put specific questions based on the witness statement and will ask the witness to answer in the same way as he or she has done before, at the time of giving the statement. This is maybe the reason why you believe that the witness answers to -- answers prepared questions, but actually the answers are already contained in the written statement. Only in exceptional cases do we have answers that were not initially in the written statement, and then you may be alerted to it and this may lead you to ask more specific questions during cross-examination. So I went really into the details of the proceedings to tell you how things really worked in practical terms. It so happens that I'm one of the Judges in this Tribunal who's been sitting non-stop in several cases for the last four years, which gives me a practical experience. Using these proceedings, I'm used to witnesses and what I'm telling you is only example of situations I've been confronted with. And they are all in compliance with the Rules and the practice of this Tribunal. Admittedly, the Tribunal could have made it impossible to have proofing sessions before testimony, but this was not done. This may be regretted but it was not done. Therefore, we have to live with it. But you too, Mr. Seselj, when the time comes for you to call your witnesses, you will have a prior meeting with every witness before the hearing and you will be able to consider with those witnesses the questions you want to put to them. Then, depending on the answers given by the witnesses during proofing, you will adjust your questions. Indeed, this procedure used by the Prosecutor can also be used by the accused, and you can do the same. Do you want to say something?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Judge, I completely understand that the -- this procedure, or rather, procedure at this Tribunal is a mixture of Anglo-Saxon and continental legal systems, but what comes under Rule 92 ter is not the result of this marriage between the two systems. It is something that has been artificially appendaged to that mixture. 92 ter does not exist anywhere, either in Anglo-Saxon law or in the continental legal system. Nowhere in the civilised world does that exist. I'm not sure that it even existed with Stalin and Hitler either. You still haven't answered my main objection. I don't have any legal certainty here, I don't feel certain and safe legally. I came to The Hague in February 2003, several days after the indictment was raised, convinced that I would be given the legal means that after an indictment can be raised the Rules of Procedure and Evidence cannot be changed to my detriment. Now it seems that I cannot rely on the law because the Rules are being endlessly changed to my detriment, and this Rule 92 ter is the most flagrant example of the amendment of the Rules of the proceedings retroactively. I was not present when any of the Prosecution witnesses were interviewed or when their statements were compiled, and that is why this is disqualified to begin with. Where I was not present or one of my representatives or perhaps Defence counsel, nothing can hold water before the Court, only the statement given, the testimony given. You know that according to the Rules you can have statements, depositions, taken, that is possible. Or the person can attend -- was -- had the right to attend but didn't wish to attend. So whenever a statement is taken without representatives of the Defence, it cannot be admitted as a document of the Court. You said that they were retired policemen who took these statements. In my country, a statement taken by a policemen without the presence of a lawyer cannot be made a court document. What policemen write is absolutely of no value for the Court and that is the same in your country, I'm sure, as it is I'm sure in the Anglo-Saxon legal system because testimony has to be made in the courtroom. The witness has to state what he has to say orally in court. Now, as I am not assured all the legal status to protect me here, then you can deal with it. But I'm not going to cooperate. I'm going to cooperate by being present when you engage in this action, but I'm not going to cooperate to the extent of acting as if I was actually cross-examining the witness properly. So look at the whole situation. All the witnesses can give statements under 92 ter, and as I said by the end of November you will have completed the whole case, but then please don't say that I have had a legal certainty and that I have been secure in the legal rights accorded to me in this court. Now, referring to the Rome Statute of the International Criminal Court, you cannot amend the rules retroactively to the detriment of the accused, so, please, I would like to hear your opinion with respect to that particular issue, and as it is stated in the Rome Statute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]... In saying that the Rules change and that the provisions that are amended in the Rules have -- operate retroactively, you are absolutely right. This is the way things happen because, you know this as well as I do, amendments were decided upon by the Judges, were introduced into the Rules, and they have a retroactive effect. This is true for Rule 92 ter. You are right in saying that the Trial Chambers apply the provisions, the amended provisions, retroactively. But here again once more, I want to reassure you, at least try to reassure you, even if I don't succeed in doing so, but this is no reason for not tackling the issue. There are guarantees in enshrined in Rule 92 ter. There are three of them, actually. I'm going to read this out again to you. All this to tell you that we do have the guarantees in place. First of all: "The Trial Chamber may admit in whole or in part the evidence of a witness in the form of a written statement." This sentence alone goes to show that the Trial Chamber is under the obligation of examining the written statement, since it can admit it in whole or in part. But this Rule also says or specifies the conditions. There are three conditions. First condition: "The witness is present in court." Do not forget that the witness has made an oath, as taken an oath, and he will testify under oath. So the first condition is that the witness is present. Second condition, the witness is available for cross-examination, this is what I told you earlier on, and any questioning by the Judges. Therefore, the Judges, too, play their part. The Judge is not just sitting passively watching this sort of tennis match between the Prosecution and the Defence. They are not spectators, they do play a part in these proceedings. You may trust the Judges. They are going to read the statements, they are going to ask themselves certain questions, and they are going to put questions to witnesses, notwithstanding the fact that the Prosecution or the Defence -- in the event that the parties would not put specific questions. So that's the second guarantee or safe-guard. The third safe-guard is as follows: "The witness attests that the written statement or transcript accurately, accurately, reflects the witness's declaration and what the witness would say if examined." This is an additional safe-guard. The witness is asked, were he or she to have to answer questions regarding the written statement, whether they would say the same and they have to say "yes" under oath, solemnly; if they were to say "no," that's the end of it. So this is the system in place, the way it operates. I can understand that you entertain some doubts as to certain witnesses, which is an additional reason for cross-examining these witnesses because you challenge some potential witnesses. That's one more reason for telling them, Look, you said this, give me an explanation. On the other hand, not forget either that there is another factor which I have mentioned already. The 92 ter proceedings usually come into play after you've had viva voce witnesses. It would be inconceivable that there would only be one or two 92 ter witnesses in order to support the allegations made by the Prosecutor in the indictment. Normally speaking, you should have viva voce witnesses. 92 ter witnesses - at least that is my experience that makes it possible for me to tell you so - generally speaking, 92 ter witnesses are victims most of the time, victims who come to speak about what they've experienced. And only very, very rarely do you have witnesses, although this is made possible by the Rules under 92 ter (B), but only very rarely so, when the witness comes to speak to the acts or conduct of the accused. So that's possible, too, but it is only very rarely used. In fact, these proceedings apply to witnesses who have been crime base victims and they do not speak to challenge the direct liability of an accused. So this is the spirit and the letter of the law. I want to say this to you, Mr. Seselj. When this Rule is implemented, it is under the control of the Judges and the Judges are going to ask themselves the same questions as you may ask yourself: Is this a credible witness? Does the witness tell the truth? Is his statement relevant? Does it have probative value? Only then -- the Judges can, and I would even venture to say they must ask questions in order to ascertain that the very conditions set out in Rule 92 ter would not prejudice the accused. I can very well understand that you want to challenge this, that you might think that you're going to be harmed in this, but this would actually not be fair for the Judges that you might think that Judges would go along in a system or with a system that would prejudice the accused in any way. That's not how I see the work of a Judge. If you feel that you're being harmed or prejudiced, I can make sure that this prejudice is dismissed and that you are restored in your rights. This is what I wanted to tell you. We will now move on to another topic -- yes, unless you have something to say. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] There are three things I would like to say, Your Honour. You have confirmed that at this trial the Rules of Procedure are retroactively amended, but I would like to hear you say whether you believe it's possible to retroactively change the Rules to the detriment of the Prosecution, that's an essential question. And among the 92 ter witnesses the Prosecution said that there will be many insiders, not victims, but associates, people who gave statements because they were threatened with indictments being brought against them. I can provide you with examples of such witnesses. You mentioned as a guarantee that this witness takes the solemn declaration -- well, the solemn declaration isn't an oath. The solemn declaration is an idea in the Serbian language is something very strange. That's the case with the Croats, Serbs and the Muslims and it has to do with the communist regime when such a declaration was taken. For example, in the pioneer's association, the pupils in the first class of school were collectively received into that communist organization, and they then gave a solemn declaration according to which they would be faithful to Tito, the communist dictator. And rest assured that no single witness who takes a solemn declaration here finds this solemn declaration something that would prevent him from lying. An oath is something else. If a man takes an oath and then commits perjury, well such a man would really be terrible, but -- although there are such cases. But a solemn declaration has never bound anyone for this Tribunal. I can guarantee that you can consult people, Serbs, Croats, or Muslims from our area or Albanians, and they will all tell you the same thing. They will all find the idea of a solemn declaration something derisory. If you continue to insist on this -- well, I have already told you what my position is. You can call many such witnesses, all the witnesses can be such witnesses, their statements can be admitted as 92 ter witnesses, I have no means of preventing that nor would I try to prevent that, apart from doing what I have already done, saying what I have already said, I won't repeat such arguments in the future. But if such witnesses are brought here I won't cross-examine them and no one else can cross-examine them on my behalf. As a Judge you can examine such witnesses and your colleagues on the Bench can examine them, although that's not a guarantee for me. Although there's nothing negative I can say about you. Personally, I can't say that you haven't acted correctly, quite the contrary. I have certain objections to certain matters. You've seen that in my recent submissions, but I can't say that you haven't acted correctly, but there are other Judges. Let me mention Judge Moloto. Here in this courtroom he asked a witness who testified about the events in Serbian Krajina. I'll paraphrase this. You Serbs from Serbian Krajina, why didn't you move out in 1990 when you knew that the Croats didn't like you there and you would have avoided the war by doing that? Judge Moloto asked such a question in the courtroom, so what kind of guarantees can I have if such Judges appear here? I have many other examples I can provide you with. There are no guarantees, so why should I trust Judges in advance? I don't trust Judges in advance. Perhaps a Judge surprises me by being very correct and then I have to admit the fact that the Judge has acted correctly, but I don't trust Judges in advance. Why should I? I tried to be an intellectual and to be an intellectual means to always doubt. Let me remind you of what Descartes said, I doubt things, my doubt is proof of my existence, so I have good reasons to have certain doubts when we are dealing with 92 ter witnesses. Do as you see fit, but I have told you what my position is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have two observations to make. On what my -- first on what my colleague, Judge Moloto said, well I don't really know what he said. Now, regarding this solemn declaration, maybe here we have an ambiguity. In the solemn declaration the witness is confirming, after having taken an oath. So first he declares that -- solemnly that he will tell the truth, and then afterwards he's asked whether if he was asked these questions again he would say the same thing. So this solemn declaration comes after taking an oath. On the second item regarding what you called insider witnesses, may I remind of our Rule 6(D) in the Rules of Procedure. Rule 6 is amendment of the rules. In paragraph (D) it says as follows: "An amendment shall enter into force seven days after the date of issue of an official Tribunal document containing the amendment but shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or of a convicted or acquitted person in any pending case." Rule 6(D) provides for retroactivity of an amendment, but also provides for this retroactivity to be subjected to the fact that the accused must in no way be prejudiced. And given this, as I said earlier, it is obvious that if Prosecution is requesting for Rule 92 ter to be applied for an important witness, the Trial Chamber must of course say no, and this has happened, it happened to me. I've already requested a witness to be viva voce, to make sure that the accused would have guarantees as to his rights. So here again, Mr. Seselj, you must trust the Bench, even if sometimes the Bench may be -- may fail, as you said, or make mistakes. But when the -- when Prosecution is asking the Bench for 92 ter to be applied, the Judges will automatically check whether the witnesses are such that this procedure may be applied, they will check whether the witness is not of a nature that obliges, that forces, the procedure to be done with an examination-in-chief and a cross-examination. This is what is required in Rule 6. Ms. Dahl, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I wanted to make some remarks regarding the application of Rule 92 ter in this case. We will bring all of our witnesses viva voce, and because of the need to use courtroom time expeditiously and the anticipated limits on the length of the Prosecution case, we will seek to supplement their oral testimony with statements in writing or prior transcripts, as permitted by Rule 92 ter. The Rule does not draw a distinction between important witnesses or less important witnesses, and in fact all of the witnesses are important; they offer testimony as to all of the elements of the crimes with which the accused is charged. We disagree with the Pre-Trial Judge's view that the written form of statement can be admitted only after cross-examination --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, Mrs. Dahl. Maybe you misunderstood me when I said that there are 92 ter witnesses as a general rule normally they're victims. Of course they're important witnesses, they're very important witnesses, but a victim is not a witness that may challenge directly the accused. However, a witness, what we call here an insider witness, so a witness belonging to a military unit or to a paramilitary unit is a witness of another nature. This witness is much closer than -- to the accused than a witness may be -- than a victim may be. So there's a difference that needs to be made. Of course all witnesses are important, but in their ranking you have different gradients. So I wanted to say this because I believe that you were -- you had misunderstood me in the first place.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't believe that there's a misunderstanding about what you said. I think that the disagreement is on the application of the Rule, with respect. We will bring all of our witnesses and seek to admit testimony in writing to supplement their courtroom time. We will allocate more courtroom time for witnesses who will testify directly to the acts and conduct of the accused. We would anticipate that that cross-examination would take longer as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute. I'm reading what you have just said at page 20, line 10, you're saying that you will bring all witnesses, which is fine, but you will seek to admit testimony in writing, but this is out of the question, Mrs. Dahl. When there is a viva voce witness, it's only the direct examination and the cross-examination and the transcript of this that is -- exists. There is no written statement. Don't mix procedures. Viva voce witness is a witness coming into the courtroom where no statement is being admitted, and I will refuse this. I can say it right away. Now, if you choose to go for Rule 92 ter, then of course the written statement will be admitted. So let's not mix things up. When a witness comes in this courtroom to testify viva voce and you've scheduled two hours for this witness, the in chief will be -- there will be an in chief for examination and a cross-examination, but no admission of a written statement. This is unheard of. However, if you bring a witness here and state prior to his testimony that he will testify under 92 ter, he may - and then I say he may - there may be a written statement but only after the fact and not before. I think this is how the system works.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is a point of serious disagreement because I believe that in this Tribunal --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, you may not agree, but this is my opinion. I am part of a Trial Chamber that will have to rule on this, and we will not admit written statements when a witness is coming to testify as viva voce. This is an accusatory procedure with an examination-in-chief and a cross-examination, together with the documents used that will be integrated into evidence and as evidence, and the statement is left aside and is not admitted. However, if you want this written statement to be admitted, then you must use Rule 92 ter or Rule 92 quater if the witness has passed away or is not able to come and testify. But this is how it works. You don't have a procedure where you have a viva voce witness and then after the fact you're asking for the written statement to be admitted. And why is that? Well, if you are calling a witness to testify for two, three, or four hours, you will put questions to this witness, of course using his written statement, but you will not go into all the items that are in this written statement. And the accused will cross-examine out of the questions that have been put to the witness during the in chief. And then if you're asking for the written statement to be admitted as evidence, there will be in this written statement some topics that will not have been debated in court. And this -- I've been a Judge here for four years. I have never admitted a written statement, as you seem to be wanting to do.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, the procedure authorised by the Rules does not preclude viva voce witnesses from having their testimony supplemented by a written statement. I'm not seeking to offer redundant evidence, but if I only have a limited amount of court time, then I need to rely on the procedures available in the Rules to supplement their written [sic] testimony. The accused has the opportunity to conduct his cross-examination based on both the oral testimony and the written statement; that is why the written statement is tendered for admission into evidence prior to the commencement of cross-examination. That is followed in every other trial of which I am aware, and it is not inconsistent with the Rules.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, I don't know where you say that this is happening. But I can tell you as far as I'm concerned I have never seen this procedure implemented with a witness coming in, Prosecution asking questions in chief, then we have a cross-examination by the Defence, the Prosecution is showing documents to the witness and of course the Prosecution will ask these documents to be admitted into evidence. But unless it's a 92 ter witness, I've never seen the Prosecution come and ask for the written statement to be admitted right away. I have never seen this happen and it has never been done, as far as I know. But what may happen, however, is that during the cross-examination the accused may challenge the credibility of the witness, and then can ask for the written statement to be admitted in order to show that the witness is not credible. This may happen, but what you're telling me I've never seen. You may ask for it, of course, but -- and the Trial Chamber will rule, but you know my position. Maybe we can move on to something else.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: One thing, all of our submissions to date have forecast this method of using court time efficiently, and it is no different than the witness coming into court and saying, Yes, this is my statement, and then tendering the witness for cross-examination. I recognise that there are some parts of a witness's testimony that should be presented orally to make sure that their testimony is complete, but if you want to have this case fairly presented regarding the Prosecution's evidence in under 150 hours, then we need to supplement the oral testimony with written evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, would you like to answer what Prosecution has just said or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Judge. First of all, I would like to agree with you that this debate of ours can be narrowed down to Rule 6(D), which states that an amendment shall not operate to prejudice the rights of the accused or a convicted or an acquitted person in any pending case. This is a pending case since February 2003, that is to say from the day the indictment was raised and my first appearance before the Court. That is pending. The case started, the proceedings started, although the trial did not start yet, and I hope there's no challenge to that. Now, the question remains of whether the retroactive application of 92 ter jeopardizes my rights as an accused or not. I claim that it does. It does jeopardize my rights because I wasn't present when the witnesses were interviewed, when their statement was taken. I wasn't able to hear whether a witness was threatened that an indictment would be raised against them if he fails to agree to make the statement. I wasn't able to hear whether any money was offered or an apartment or house in some third country so that he could take refuge there with his family, whether he was offered employment as an enticement. Those are all methods that the Prosecution uses in order to get witnesses, and I have a problem because they promised employment or money to certain witnesses and didn't keep their promises. And then these disillusioned witnesses don't wish to come in and testify. I know there are some cases in point like that. So I'm saying that with the application of Rule 92 ter my rights and interests are being jeopardized, they do come under threat, and let's see what your position is, do you think that they do not? What Ms. Dahl has just said shows that the Prosecution, in fact, wishes to apply a mixture of the Rules of Evidence and hearing witnesses viva voce and 92 ter. They would like to may a new marriage, a new mixture, that every witness is viva voce, a little bit viva voce, and a little bit under Rule 92 ter. That's what they want to do, and we can see that from these numerous requests that they have made and this is something that Ms. Dahl confirmed here. And I need to know in advance for each and every witness whether he is going to be a viva voce witness and will be a viva voce witness in his entirety or is he a 92 ter witness and will be heard exclusively under Rule 92 ter. They have to clear that up before the start of trial and before the witness appears here in court. I have to know whether he's a viva voce witness or whether he's a 92 ter witness. If he's a viva voce witness, then I will prepare to cross-examine him very extensively. If it's a Rule 92 ter witness, I will ignore his testimony. However, if all witnesses are going to be a mixture of Rule 92 ter and viva voce, then we have a new terrible problem raising its ugly head here, and I hope that you're not going to agree to their requests and won't give in to those requests; that would be the most terrible thing, not something that even I could have imagined was going to happen. Although any apocalyptic vision is something that my brain can envisage.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Ms. Dahl, I have a question. I should have put it to you before but I was thinking of other things, so I didn't. When you're going to call a witness, X or Y or Z, normally speaking, at least this is the way your colleagues work. They inform the counsel, the Defence counsel, beforehand - in this case you'll have to tell Mr. Seselj since he's representing himself - you've got to tell them that this is going to be a viva voce or a 92 ter witness. This is generally what all your colleagues do. Are you planning to do the same?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, I disagree with the premise of the statement that my colleagues are applying labels to witnesses. We have already on file more than 60 applications for admission of evidence in writing, and I know the number because I just recapitulated all of them at the Court's direction, there are 64 of them plus there are additional motions under Rule 92 quater. All of our witnesses will come to court and we will seek to admit additional evidence in writing to supplement what they say in court. Now, it may be that the efficient use of courtroom time limits their testimony to the following questions: Is this your statement? Would you say the same thing today under oath if you were questioned -- if the same questions were put to you, would you give the same answers? That will be exceptionally brief. We will disclose in advance the statement, the relevant exhibits that we will tender through the witness, and it will follow the pattern that we have already set forth in the 64 motions that have already been filed before the Chamber. The Pre-trial Chamber has not issued any decisions on those motions, and in re capitulating them and in view of Mr. Seselj's express desire to exercise his right to cross-examination, we will not proceed on the basis of Rule 92 bis which is to accept written statement in lieu of oral testimony. The Rules fully authorise the presentation of viva voce evidence and the admission of additional evidence of the witness in writing, and that is how we will proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I take due note of what you have said. My colleagues will have an opportunity to discuss this, and we may come back to this during the Pre-Trial Conference, which leads me to talk about the composition of the Bench. Mr. Seselj, I am used to full transparency, I have always been fully transparent and I shall remain so. A Trial Chamber is going to be established so that as early as on the 6th of November there will -- there can be a Pre-Trial Conference with a Chamber; and on the 7th and the 8th of November, we'll have the preliminary statement by Ms. Dahl and by you. You will be speaking on the 8th of November. Now, what is the make-up of the Trial Chamber? The President of the Tribunal sees the Secretary-General of the United States [as interpreted] so that two Ad Litem Judges be nominated and appointed. They are currently in the Bench of the Delic case. The President of the Tribunal asked the Judges to be appointed by the 15th of October. We are beyond that date and we still have no answer from the UN Secretary-General. Whatever the situation may be, we shall have an answer and we shall, therefore, have a Trial Chamber, and I will be the Presiding Judge as of the 6th of November. As I told you last time, there are several cases and there are only three courtrooms, so I really had to fight to make sure that the three days, 6th, 7th, and 8th of October [as interpreted] would be days that we would have Courtroom I or Courtroom III for. Now, as to the coming days after the 8th of November, for the time being there is no absolute certainty, but in theory we should be able to start with the first witnesses on the 4th of December, the Tuesday; on Wednesday, 5th of December; and on Thursday, 6th of December. Thereafter, we might have Tuesday, 11 December; Wednesday, 12; and Thursday, 13 of December. And then we would resume in January after the winter recess. One thing is basically certain. The dates of the 11th, 12th, and 13th of December are sure. As to the 4th, 5th, and 6th of December, it's on a stand-by basis because it may be that one of the Ad Litem Judges may be taken up by another case; if this is so, we could have another -- we could have a solution provided for by the Rules. Because when a Judge is absent for a justifiable ground, the proceedings may continue with only two Judges. It is not necessary to have the three Judges of the Bench, be it only in the Milosevic case you sometimes had two and not three Judges. But of course the absent Judge is informed by the Presiding Judge of what happened during the hearing, and the Judge receives the transcript and their related documents discussed during the hearing. So this is a possible, if not likely, schedule. Therefore, the Prosecution will have to prepare witnesses for the -- or the first witness for the 4th of December. As a result, Ms. Dahl, I'd like to draw your attention to the following problem, and it's entirely up to you; however, I have to speak to this. As you know, we'll only have three hearing days in a week for two reasons, because this was requested by Mr. Seselj so that he can represent himself. Another reason is that I, myself, I'm sitting on another case, and I'm not going to have ten hearings a week, sitting on two cases. So there should be, therefore, less hearing days. As a consequence, we can only sit three hearing days a week, and it's very clear in my mind, on Tuesdays, Wednesdays, and Thursdays. But I have a problem. If you were to call a witness on Thursday who is scheduled to testify over two days, that witness will have to stay here in The Hague on Friday, Saturday, Sunday, and Monday; in other words, he will have to stay here for those days with accommodation to be paid as well as allowance for the witness. In order to avoid this type of situation, please take into account that you have make sure that you call witnesses during those three days without them having to stay on unduly. How? Well, you can plan a witness for three days. He could sit -- he could testify for two days and the second one for one day, or still a witness to testify over three days. But if you call two witnesses for the three days, one taking two days and the other one two days as well, inevitably it will spill over. I know it's not an easy thing to do at all. You have to be extremely precise, like clockwork. But if you are in the OTP, you can incorporate all these factors so that you avoid having a witness who stays for days on end which has financial repercussions. So I don't think it is impossible to do so regarding a number of witnesses. You can make sure that over a three-day week you have two witnesses, one to testify over two days and the other one over one day. It may be that you only have witnesses who testify for a day. You could then have three witnesses in that week. At any rate, I seem to understand and I think you said so yourself already, you also want to use the time efficiently, you want to be efficient in court time. So a hearing day is four hours, if you remove all procedural matters that may arise. So in four hours you should have two hours for your examination-in-chief and the Defence would have two hours for their cross-examination, so that's manageable. And two hours, that's quite a lot for a witness. Therefore, you can call three witnesses per week, provided each witness does not take up more than two hours for the direct examination because if you do so Mr. Seselj will have the same time as you. So if you need three or four hours for a witness, he too will have the same amount of time. So it's up to you. You have to take that into account, see to it. I could always with my colleagues, with the fellow Judges, give you some instructions, some guide-lines in this matter, but it would be disastrous to have the end of the day on Thursday and for us to tell the witness that he has to come back only on Tuesday, the next week, he would have to wait. So wisdom would have it that in a week a witness, if you plan two days for him or her, you call him on Tuesday and Wednesday then have another witness on the Thursday. Don't start the one plan for two days for him to start on the last day, but you know this as well as I do. This is just an observation, knowing how difficult it is, because you have to take into account the availability of the witness as well as the scheduling requirements. But the I'm sure we'll have an opportunity to get back to this. Earlier on you mentioned 150 hours. I don't know what the Bench will decide when we have the Pre-Trial Conference, will it be 150 or 120 hours, I can't tell you right now, because this is a decision to be made by the full Bench. In this regard my fellow Judges will have their say, but as far as I can see your request seems to be a reasonable one, quite an appropriate one. But of course if you are given 120 or 150 hours, Mr. Seselj will have the same amount of time, since we have the principle of the equality of arms prevailing here. So the Judges will sum up the hours, as provided in the Rule 65 ter chart and will see whether the number of hours should be reduced or increased. But at first sight, it seems that we should spend the first half here of 2008 with the Prosecution case, and we should start the Defence case of course notwithstanding submissions under 98 bis, after the summer recess, so in August. And the last six months of 2008 and maybe the first quarter of 2009, so this is the general outline, but I'm sure that this will be discussed again during the Pre-Trial Conference. My fellow Judges will have to make a determination as well, and sometimes, you know that well, Trial Chambers reduce the time. And if the Prosecution is not happy with it, they will file a motion for -- to reconsider or a motion for certification of appeal, and then the Appeals Chamber will have to say whether the Trial Chamber applied its discretionary power properly or not and did not make any mistake. So this is what might happen if there were to be challenges. But to be clear, I believe that Trial Chamber I had initially granted 81 hours to the Prosecution, I may be wrong about this, but I seem to remember that number. Very well. So this is what I wanted to say regarding the Bench and its composition. As soon as the President of the Tribunal hears from the UN Secretary-General, he'll issue an order establishing the composition of the Trial Chamber, and this order will of course be made known to Mr. Seselj as soon as it is issued so that Mr. Seselj be informed of the composition of the Trial Chamber. Before the break, we have another ten minutes left. Yes, Mr. Seselj, you have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I won't need ten minutes, Judge. First of all, in principle I am -- I hear that you say that the Ad Litem Judges will be appointed, and I'm amazed that in less than a month they will be able to get to know all the files and documents of this court, but that's just my surprise and amazement that I wanted to express. But I'd like to draw your attention to some other things that haven't been fulfilled. You took the decision whereby the names of a certain number of protected witnesses should be disclosed to me 30 days prior to the commencement of trial; that has not been done. And in my opinion, sanctions should be taken now against the representatives of the Prosecution and you could perhaps along those lines prohibit them bringing those witnesses because they failed to disclose their names a month before trial. I don't know what other measures could be taken that would not jeopardize my rights in the proceedings. Secondly, not all the exhibits have been disclosed to me, especially the confidential ones, and some expert reports as well. You will recall that there was a decision whereby the confidential part of Theunens's expert report should be disclosed to me 14 days before the start of trial, that was not done. They did, however, disclose part of that report by the expert witness, but not the confidential parts and the part that was left out last time; that has not been disclosed. And I have not received material pursuant to Rule 68(i). The Prosecution recognised in its document that it has to provide me with 400.000 pages, and they tried to disclose them to me on e-court, in electronic format, or in English, but they have not done what they said they would do to date. I am still receiving certain exhibits and documents exclusively in English. Sometimes I receive empty files. There are 150 such to date and some -- for some exhibits they say that they're going to postpone disclosure, there are quite a number of those, several hundred, in fact, which have not yet been disclosed. So that job has not been completed, and I don't know whether under such conditions the proceedings can begin at all. Now, as far as I'm concerned, I'm trial-ready, and we could go ahead tomorrow. I won't do anything to raise any objections, but I'd just like to tell you that the Prosecution has not met the prerequisites, procedural ones, for the start of trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, you raised various issues. I'll deal with them later on, but there's one thing I'd like to deal with in the time remaining before the break, it's not very long indeed. On the 16th of October, 2007, I issued a decision on the motion by the Prosecution to reconsider the decision on protective measures. I shall not go into the contents of the decision on protective measures, since it is a confidential decision. However, in this decision I took a decision as to the meaning to be given by the expression "30 days before the final date for the commencement of trial." In the decision I said the said expression had to be understood as meaning 30 days before the date set for the commencement of the Prosecution case. Therefore -- well, the beginning of the Prosecution case is due to begin on the 4th of December. The 30 days before that date make it compulsory for the Prosecution to disclose the list at the latest on the 4th of November. We're not there yet. So this is a reasoned decision. That may be the reason why you did not have it translated into your language. And in this decision I ruled on this matter of the 30-day time-limit. As far as I'm concerned, before the first Prosecution witness arrives, you need to have the list of these witnesses of the protected witnesses whose names and other particulars you do not yet know. So this matter, this issue, is dealt with in the 16 October 2007 decision that explains what is to be understood by the expression of the 30-day limit, that is, the 30 days before the first Prosecution witness comes. If for some extraordinary reason we were not to sit on the 4th of December, of course the date would be accordingly shifted. But I can tell you that for the time being we plan to sit on the 4th of December because by then the Judges will have been appointed. You said how admiring you were of the fact that in a matter of days the Ad Litem Judges could familiarise themselves with the entire case file. Mr. Seselj, I have to tell you that further to Rule 65 ter (L) I've prepared for the Ad Litem Judges a report that I am under the obligation of giving them. It is ready. I only have to put the Judges' names and to sign it. This report will inform my colleagues of the entire proceedings until now and will inform them of the decisions issued so far. I'll speak about the Status Conferences, the amendments of the indictment, the preliminary motions, the special defence, the agreement on facts, the issue of financing the defence, the problems related to the disclosure of exhibits, protective measures, the issue of transcript under 92 bis, 92 ter, and 92 quater, the issue of contempt, Rule 77, practical matters regarding trial management, problems to do with translation, transport of exhibits, the e-court system, et cetera. In other words, the Judges will receive a complete and comprehensive report taking stock of the proceedings so far. Therefore, after reading the record, the Judges will be fully apprised and fully operational. This is what I wanted to tell you. It is now 10.30. We're going to break for 20 minutes and we shall resume in 20 minutes' time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. Mr. Seselj, I would now like to deal with the question of your associates. I don't know where you stand now. I don't know whether they will assist you during the trial. Among the three associates, did you tell the registry which one was lawyer in Belgrade? Do you have any problems? Is Mrs. Ragus here? So could you tell us where you stand right now. I want to deal with this issue because I felt that you had to be helped. So what can you tell me as far as your associates are concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, first of all I have to comment on something with regard to what you were saying just before the break, with your leave, I will be very brief, and then I could answer your question. Six months ago I was very surprised by your very correct approach to the procedural problems in this case; that was the case at the first Status Conference in March. Now I'm quite surprised by your interpretation of your own decision which is against the legal provisions. At the beginning of the proceedings -- well, the beginning of the proceedings I thought should begin with the Prosecution's opening statement. Now you're saying that the beginning of the proceedings commences on the first day that the Prosecution starts to present its case, call its witnesses, and that's what I wanted to say. I'm surprised by this position, but I'll move on. My associates won't be present in The Hague in the course of the proceedings. They'll be in Belgrade. They'll comply with their usual duties, they'll do what they do to make a living, and when they have free time and to the extent that they do have free time, they'll assist me with my defence. I'll have phone contact with them, because the question of how the defence will be financed has not been resolved. It hasn't been solved because the registry set some impossible conditions for me to meet. If you like, I could go into greater detail with regard to what the registry's asking of me. I don't know whether you have seen the registry's letter of the 28th of September of this year, it consists of six densely typed pages and it's signed by Martin Petrov, assistant for legal affairs. And you can see in this letter why your decision on financing the Defence won't be implemented. I'm asked to inform the registry of the property situation with regard to my entire family, and the registry says on the basis of that information, on the basis of the resources available to you, the registry shall take -- shall deduct certain costs in relation to the Defence that should be financed by the applicant. Documents on the house that my family lives in, it belongs to my family, they want the title for the house, they want to see how much was paid by my mother for the house. It's a house that she inherited, and they want to see how many funds we used for renovation. This house was bought 20 years ago. It's impossible to obtain such documents. Even if I wanted to obtain such documents, it would be impossible to do so. In the 1980s and 1990s, buying private property in Serbia was something that was done by paying in cash alone; it wasn't done through bank accounts, through intermediaries. Tax wasn't established on the basis of the price reported, it was done on the basis of an official assessment. So am I to inform the registry of how my mother obtained the financial resources to buy such property? Well, this is ridiculous. I'm not going to deal with some such request. Something similar has been asked of my wife. According to the information I provided the registry with, my sister and two aunts now live in the house that is the property of my wife because we did an exchange, as my family is large, I have four sons, a wife, a sister-in-law, two grandsons. My mother gave us a greater, a larger, house and my wife gave her sister, my sister, a smaller house. They are now asking for documents that show that my wife paid for the house with her own financial resources, house she got from her father, that she had aid from my sister, that she obtained funds for the renovation, extension of the house. Well, my wife didn't even want to give me such information when I was in Belgrade, let alone now that I've been absent from Belgrade for five years. The information here is incorrect. The house I live in is a house of 300 square metres. 12 times 10 metres are the dimensions of the foundation. That's the space that can be used, but they also included two garages and a basement and a two terraces around the house as if that should be included. That would add up to a total of 437 square metres. And now, since I don't have a vehicle of any kind, I had two, one was a Toyota from 1990 and another was a Volvo from 1995. The Toyota isn't road-worthy and the other one, the other vehicle, was sold by my son, he needed the money for his family. Now they want me to provide them with information on the vehicles owned by other family members. My wife in the meantime has bought a car, but you don't think she's going to provide me with information about that, do you, so that I could forward such information to the registry; I won't do that. Then they are asking for other information. I'll summarize this. I don't want to go into detail. Since I informed the Tribunal of something, you know when I was imposed stand-by lawyer, Aleksandar Lazarevic from Belgrade for a certain period of time, well I then engaged investigators who looked into his family history and how he was engaged so that I could discredit such an imposed lawyer. I did that successfully and he himself asked to be withdrawn. He said he would prosecute me because there's a conflict of interest, and as soon as this matter was dealt with he didn't even think of filing a complaint against me. In one of the submissions to the registry I stated that I had paid 20.000 euros to obtain all that information. And now the registry is asking me to provide information on whom I paid the sum to. They want bank statements. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: Now I'm asking for a photocopy of the passport to show, demonstrate, that this investigator travelled to Macedonia. So they want to know who this investigator is and how this investigator obtained such information. That's what they are most concerned with. And naturally they want bank statements, but I didn't use banks to make such payments. Perhaps it didn't even cost a full 20.000 euros, but I rounded this figure up. It certainly cost a certain amount. It was certainly necessary to pay a certain sum of money. I have provided information on my property. I won't do that for my family property, and if you can read through the entire text - I don't want to go into everything, it's a little tiring - you will then see that impossible conditions have been set for me. So I have drawn a conclusion from this, and my Defence will, quite simply, not be financed; I can see that. They have known since I arrived in The Hague 22 of my books have been published -- many more have been published; in fact, 30, over 30, but those books were published by the Serbian Radical Party. I didn't receive a fee of any kind, and the party usually distributes these books freely because the purpose of the books is to engage in propaganda against the Tribunal. There are scientific conferences that are held and when they are sold the price is symbolic. The books cost less than it cost to have them printed. Now they want certificates about the books sold, about the situation in the warehouse, and so on and so forth, and they even want me to provide them with bank statements on the transactions of the committee for the Defence of Vojislav Seselj; in 2003 or 2004 I provided them with such statements, with such bank statements. And I then provided them with a detailed work-plan of the committee for my defence. This isn't a committee that's defending me before the Tribunal; it's a committee for my defence before the international public. And there I listed the tasks of the committee. Firstly, in front of the Serbian -- in front of Serbia and in front of the international community they are supposed to demonstrate the illegal foundations of the Tribunal for the former Yugoslavia. That's in my letter to the registry of the 7th of December, 2004, submission 62. Secondly, its purpose is to present arguments to demonstrate that this is an anti-Serbian Tribunal, and this can be seen from the ethnic affiliation of the accused and from the judgements in which general political and historical facts are erroneously interpreted. And then I also mentioned Zionist factions led by George Soros, Ms. Albright, and so on and so forth; and I also mentioned the fact that as an accused my rights should be respected and the Tribunal and its bodies systematically violate my rights and its purpose are also to contact international organizations. It should also organize scientific and legal conferences to discuss all the aspects of the case against me, and they are also to discuss the illogical premises of the Tribunal that pose a risk to international law as a whole. The first such conference was on the 21st of September, 2003. There have been over ten such conferences, over ten in Belgrade, and a certain number of conferences in Serbia, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, this is very interesting, but regarding the proof of your lack of financial resources of indigence, I must draw the conclusion that until now you have not provided the registry with what it required. You have told us at length what -- why you didn't, but one question I should have asked you is the following: I guess that your wife files a tax statement. Does your wife file a tax statement and are you on this tax statement also? And if that's the case, then in this document we must find your financial situation as far as taxes are concerned. So does your wife file a tax return?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, first of all, the documents my wife has are documents I have no access to. I will never have access to them unless someone in my name takes them from my wife by force. Secondly, all official documents of official bodies of the Government of Serbia are documents that the registry has. I never had a single secret bank account. All the accounts I had were open. They can obtain such information from the MUP, from the Ministry of Finance, from the inland revenue, and so on and so forth. I've provided information, all information, about my own property. I did that a few years ago. I'm now being asked to do something that doesn't concern me personally. What I'm being requested to do concerns people whose will I cannot control, even if they are my closest relatives, because none of them participated in any of my alleged war crimes. And my wife and children don't want to live in a tent, they don't want to sell the house to finance my defence. They're not prepared to do that. And the house, given its surface, isn't larger than what one needs. It's nothing luxurious. The registry could have looked into all of these matters, and I believe that the registry has done so. But this letter wasn't drafted in good faith in order to solve the problem. It just presents an obstacle that is insurmountable. Your interpretation is not correct. I didn't refuse to provide the registry with all the information they required. I provided them with all the information they required about my own property, but I don't want to look into the property situation of others, even if they are my closest relatives, and no one can ask me to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, if I understood you right, as of today, even though this decision on financing occurred some months ago, your associates still are not paid and because of this they will not come to The Hague; that's the conclusion you drew from this, right?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Perhaps the interpretation wasn't quite right. The interpreter said that they hadn't been paid because they wouldn't be coming to The Hague. It's the reverse they won't be coming to The Hague because they're not being paid for their work. They will continue to assist my defence to the extent they can do so in their free time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. I've just identified an important problem. Last time when we met we talked about the transportation of your documents for the hearing, and the possibility was that one of your associates would come to get them, transport them, circulate them, and bring them back. But if you have no associate, no one can transport these documents and we have another problem. So on December 4th, how are you going to solve this issue of transportation? If you come with 10 or 12 binders, who is going to carry them and transport them if you have no associates present in court?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The registry has to solve that problem. You probably received their letter dated the 30th of August which I was provided with on the 7th of September. They say that the transport of this material is impossible, and I believe that it is possible if the registry and the Dutch police demonstrate good-will. In the van they used to transport me around, well they have a lot of room for a lot of material, as you can see. I have a larger brief-case now and the binders I will be provided with -- that I will need for cross-examination have to be provided for me. So this will represent an expense for the registry. Perhaps they will have to pay a Dutch policeman a little more. Perhaps they will need another two security guards, but this is a problem that they have to deal with, that they have to solve. My documents must be with me at all times, and if there is someone who is carrying these documents for me, I have to be able to see this person. I don't want anyone tampering with my documents. These are problems that the registry can resolve very easily if they don't want to complicate matters. According to this letter from the registry, you can see that they were just creating difficulties. John Hocking, the deputy registrar signed this submission. They want to create difficulties, but these difficulties can be avoided. I'm not asking for anything impossible to be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This is what I will do. I will have a new meeting with them to try and find a solution to this problem. As you are -- from what you're telling us, I note that your associates are going to stay in Belgrade and you're going to be alone here in The Hague. I would like now to come back to what you said earlier regarding the beginning of the trial. You seem to be surprised that the date on which the trial starts is when the first witness comes. Chapter 6 of the rule is titled: "Trial," and there is a section 1 and section 2 you have the whole procedure of the trial and you have Rule 82, which deals with joint and separate trials; then Rule 83: Instruments of restraint, this is irrelevant in our case; but as far as Rule 84 is concerned, however, here you have the case presentation because you have the opening statement in Rule 84. "Before presentation of evidence by the Prosecutor, each party may make an opening statement." Therefore, Mr. Seselj, this is how the trial occurs. When you look at Rule 84, you see that the trial will start with Rule 84, opening statement, and then you have Rule 85: Presentation of evidence with the witnesses. This is how it occurs. Therefore, the trial -- the start of the trial is provided for in section 2, case presentation, and as far as I'm concerned the 30 days start running before the first witness is called. This is how the rule should be interpreted. However, I must tell you that there are no rules in the regulation that set the date for the beginning of the trial; it's only a matter of interpretation of these rules. When you look, however, at national practices and what is done in national jurisdictions, the hearing -- the trial starts when you have the first hearing with the first witnesses, when the accused starts answering questions, and so on. This is when the trial starts. Trial doesn't start while it's still in the Status Conference procedure; this is only a procedural step. The trial starts when you have the opening statements provided for in Rule 84 and then the presentation of evidence with witnesses. But I wanted to mention this, but I must say that it is true that the Rules of Procedure and Evidence are not very specific as to the start of the trial, and you have to really look at the title of section 1, case presentation, as well as section 1 of chapter 6 to note that the trial is provided for in the regulation but nothing is said about the beginning of trial. But normally, beginning of trial is when you have the presentation of the cases, of course with the calling of witnesses. This, I hope, answers your question as to the beginning of trial. Then there's another important issue that I would like to address, which is the translation of your book. This is what happened. You wrote a lengthy book, more than a thousand pages, written in Cyrillic. The book was turned over to the registry for translation because it is a right you're entitled to. Now, our translation services, through a letter written by the registry, told me about a problem. Their problem is that it is absolutely impossible to translate such a large book, such a long book. Furthermore, they said that one person can translate four pages a day. So for a book of that length you see that translation will take an extremely long time, and to translate such a book according to the practice, obviously would take a year if there was only one person working on the translation. And even if you recruit a translator and pay him 3.000 or 4.000 euros a month, altogether the Tribunal would have to spend between 30.000 and 40.000 euros to translate the book. So your book really was a problem for us. And secondly, asking only the index to be -- a table of contents to be translated, I found out that there were chapters that may have a great importance for your case. So I ruled, and in my ruling I asked you to tell us which paragraphs and which pages in that book which may be relevant to your case. So this is what I meant by my ruling. However, despite the fact that this book should be translated, I don't see how we could find a solution to the problem. The research done to find out whether the Tribunal had already translated books showed us that before 2001 only two very short books had been translated, and this was before 2001. We also found out that two other books had been translated outside the Tribunal and were just reviewed by our linguistic section. Therefore, before 2001, that was eight years ago, only two very short books were translated by our services; and since then, no book whatsoever was translated by our services. This is how things stand now. I fully understand that in your book there may be chapters that the Bench must know about and which you may use during your cross-examinations. But have we solved the problem? Of course as far as you're concerned you may -- maybe have some kind of publishing contract with a British publisher in order for this publishing house to translate your book and publish it in the US or in the UK or wherever, and then we would have an English translation. But apart from this, unless you translate it yourself -- but you told us earlier that you were an indigency, so I believe it's totally impossible that you could translate this yourself. So I don't see how you could find a solution. Now, Mr. Seselj, is that an infringement on your rights as an accused? This is an administrative problem, a logistics problem. This would force the Tribunal to spend money that it does not have. The translation department is ready to translate some chapters, but you must tell the translation services what chapters need to be translated. It's up to you to tell them. This is your case and I'm not supposed to interfere with your case. At one point in time I'm sure that in the table of contents I saw a chapter called "Greater Serbia," now, this may be relevant to your case and then you can ask the registry to have this translated by CLSS. I just briefly reviewed the table of contents and I was under the impression that your book scans the whole era. It's probably extremely interesting, but I'm sure that in the book there are paragraphs or chapters that are fully relevant to your case but it's up to you to identify them. I think that the book is more than 500 pages long. So asking for 500 pages to be fully translated is a daunting task, it's almost an impossible mission. Mr. Seselj, you have the floor. What is your solution? What can you tell us as far as this is concerned?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, the first time the registry talked to me about exhibits and Defence documents and that they should be translated on time, I informed the representative of the registry that I would have a total of approximately 10.000 pages of relevant documents which needed to be translated.
