Of those 10.000 pages there are two books, numbering 1.000 pages each, and the rest are various other documents relating to various trials, legal proceedings, people who committed crimes that are being ascribed to me, ranging up to official documents and statements testifying to the fact that persons who have been accused of certain crimes were not volunteers of the Serbian Radical Party and that I could possibly be behind them on the battle-field. So the exhibits and documents as opposed to the Prosecution, I have reduced them to the most relevant and the most necessary; I have made a selection. And since I stand accused here of a crime that never existed before in international criminal practice, and that is hate speech -- speech of hatred and inciting hatred, hate speech, that is why I have to defend myself against this crime of hate speech. It is my thesis that I never applied hate speech despite the fact that anyway I questioned the existence of such a crime in the first place. The book about Roman Catholic crimes and -- related to the Croatian people proves that the Croats of today are a nation that has been thought up and that hate speech is impossible if you want to prove that such a nation does not exist. The Croats of today derive from the Serbs upon which Catholicism was imposed, just as the Muslims were derived from Serbs to whom Islam was imposed in previous centuries and they all speak the Serbian language. It only happened to us Serbs that those parts of the changing their nation under religious threat become the representatives of an artificial nation. Can you imagine French people in France taking on Islam and say they are no longer French men their Muslims by virtue of their nationality and ethnicity. So through this book I prove the facts, I say that these converts, turncoats, after a long period of time are regularly used as instruments in the hands of the Serb's enemies, the Vatican, Austria, Hungary, Turkey, America, the European Union, and ultimately the NATO pact. They are always somebody else's instruments against the Serb's enemies. So without this book in its entirety, I am not able to prove that in a proper manner. I have published thus far 101 books, and of those 101 books I am getting ready to demand that only two books be translated. One is the Ideology of Serb Nationalism, in which I have concentrated all my nationalistic and idea logical viewpoints. The Prosecution has already had a third of that book translated based on its own selection and supplied me with those parts but I would like the other two-thirds of that book to be translated as well because if you reject the translation of the book the project of an artificial Croatian nation and the Roman Catholic church then there's no pointed in me presenting you any other evidence and documents. I will be using documents when I come to examine witnesses and whether you're going to accept them and admit them into evidence is irrelevant as far as I'm concerned because exhibits have never been disqualified in advance, Defence exhibits and documents in advance, as you did with this book. So I ask that your decision be thought out again. Now, as far as translation is concerned, I don't know what the methods used here are and that for a whole working day only four pages are translated. I know that in my country the situation is quite different. I know that you can bring other translators from outside for much less money, much less than the exaggerated money being paid to translators here for whatever reasons, I don't want to enter into that, I will of course defend myself even if the book has not been translated, but then no Defence documents will be translated either because I won't submit them anyway, so that's the situation we will be facing. I have no other way of responding to this. You said up to 1991, or rather, 2001 only two books have been translated and that afterwards no other works were translated. My information tells me differently. I know that Simo Zaric's book has been translated in the trial of the Samac group. I know that other books were translated for other trials, whereas the Prosecution translated for me and sent me two books by Borislav Jovic which have almost nothing to do with this trial. The first book is "The Last Days of the SFRY" and it numbers about 500 pages and the other book is his book about Slobodan Milosevic where he continues his inter-party conflict with Milosevic in the book because Milosevic threw him out of the Socialist Party. So these books are relevant and they should be translated and sent to me it seems, but books which are a reflection of my entire ideology don't seem to be relevant, well don't translate them then, whereas you have translated those two. There are textbooks that have been translated by the military academy, the command and staff academy textbooks, and general -- training schools for generals. Those textbooks have been translated, constitutions, laws have been translated, whereas the registry has refused and you have refused to have what I consider to be exceptionally relevant translated. So I don't know how that is possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I'm not refusing anything. You say that I'm refusing things. No, I don't. That's not the problem. You have a book that is 1.000 pages long, 1.000 pages, and you're even planning a second book. And I'm just learning this. This is why Status Conferences are useful because it makes it possible to really identify problems. So there is a second book also 1.000 pages long apparently, but you say one-third of it has been translated by the OTP and there are two-thirds of it that have not been translated. And you think this book is important because it expresses your views, your ideas on nationalistic ideology, so this book, too, could be relevant. Your two books might be relevant, I agree with you on that. And needless to say, if they were translated, it would be a useful thing to do. But the problem is that for them to be translated you need to be able to do it. You need the resources. You explained to me that altogether for your Defence you had 10.000 pages. If I understood properly, there are at least 2.000 pages taken up by the two books, so there would be another 8.000 pages devoted to other matters, topics, which too seem interesting to me. You talked about judgements against individuals who were alleged to have committed crimes, and you say they do not belong to your movement. Of course all this is interesting, and it would be only normal for such documents to be tendered into evidence. Yet, the question that is arising here is as follows: Does the registry find itself in a situation where it can really translate 10.000 pages? For the time being the answer that was given to me by CLSS is that they can't do it. They told me that they'd made an extra effort in order to recruit people on a provisional basis for all your submissions to be translated and for all the OTP motions to be translated into your language or so -- or the expert reports so that you have all the evidence you need. But listening to you, I am under the impression that this part of your own defence was, if not ignored, or at least not taken enough into consideration. Very shortly I shall have a meeting with the CLSS and other organs in this Tribunal in order to find a way out, what can be done to comply with your rights. But believe me, and I'm saying this again, I never intended to curtail you of any rights, but I as you or as the Prosecutor, we may be faced with insurmountable problems. And if that is the case, we have to find practical solutions or even pragmatic solutions. And if you want to be practical or pragmatic, one of the solutions would be that out of the thousand pages in your book you would select some parts, some chapters which are particularly useful to your case. Indeed, Mr. Seselj, do not forget. I said this again -- I've said this already, but I have to recall you, that in the last instance when the Bench will have to determine itself on the basis of the Prosecution evidence and on the basis of the Defence evidence, they will have to rule beyond reasonable doubt, and their findings will be based on documents, on book excerpts, on witness testimony, and also on everything that came out of the questioning and the adversarial system here playing out in court. Then, either by way of footnotes, references can be made to your books. And if it is a particularly important point it will be in the body of the trial judgement. But you are the only one who knows what is relevant, I don't, because I do not know the book. All I know about it is the table of contents. You gave an outline of your thesis and you said that it was a useful thing for you. I do not doubt it, but what I'm saying is that if one wants to appreciate the relevance of it one must be able to read what you have written and one needs the translation of what you have written, failing which when a witness is called, for instance, expert Oberschall, you will have to cross-examine and possibly contradict him and also if your book is not translated because the Prosecutor will be on her feet and will say that they have not received in English the translation of relevant paragraphs. And the Bench will also be totally confused in the ignorance, in the dark. So I'll meet again with CLSS, and during the Pre-Trial Conference, because that's also one of the purposes of such a Pre-Trial Conference, I shall tell you the outcome of the meeting, what the registry can commit itself to. I am trying to find a solution that would satisfy you because the worst thing would be for you to believe, be it for one minute, that you are prevented from defending yourself. I've said that a number of times and I say it once again, never was it my intention. I shall do everything that is possible for you to have the feeling at the end of the trial that you were listened to and that you were able to defend yourself; otherwise, you would have been right to say that you were prevented from defending yourself. So please look again into this matter. I will discuss this with the registry, and during the Pre-Trial Conference I shall deal with this again. Because I think that this issue had some repercussions because you said that you were not going to give your documents for e-court purposes, for them to be filed, if your book was not translated. Was that some kind of reprisal or retribution or because you wanted to show your discontent, I don't know, Mr. Seselj, but know that witnesses who are called and you wish to cross-examine them with your own documents sooner or later will need those documents. So I just remind you of this point. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I have absolutely no intention of any reprisals or measures of retribution, and I'm not in a position to do so, although maybe I would apply a reprisal if I was in a position to do so, but I'm not. Because you have the whole situation under your control and I'm not complaining about that. In 2003 already I sent the Prosecution here in the courtroom, in this courtroom and some other courtroom, I brought into court and the guards carried it with their very own hands 80 of my books, first editions. They were soft-cover books and a little narrower than the present ones. And the Prosecution has had almost five years to read through all those books and to set aside certain portions and excerpts as Prosecution documents. So I went out of my way to be very correct and proper. I brought the books myself and handed them over to them, and much of those books have been translated and I think that you've already received those translations in English. They are my interviews to newspapers, debates on television, speeches in the Assembly, speeches at political meetings, and so on and so forth. That's what those books comprise. Now, if I was malicious and had ill-intent, I would insist that all these books be translated in their entirety because the Prosecution selected excerpts, but I'm not malicious. All I'm asking for is two basic fundamental books be translated, they're not by speeches, not my interviews on television or anything else, they are books I wrote with my own hand and which almost wholly express my entire ideology, the ideology that I advocate. And in my opinion you should be just in your conduct, and to be just in your conduct does not mean merely assessing the resources of the registry, but how much the Prosecution has been able to supply documents and how many documents were able to be translated into English or a few of them from English into Serbian. I'm a very modest man with respect to the Prosecution. I have modest means, but I would have the right to insist upon the same amount, which I'm not doing. I've reduced everything to a total of about 10.000 pages. So the problem is easily resolved. There are very serious agencies dealing in translation and speak off the bat, but in Belgrade if you have an agency to translate anything it costs 10 to 20 euros, so if there was good intent on the part of the registry they would have asked around to see where the most suitable agencies exist and then calculated the costs based on that. Those translations are professional, but it's not up to me to secure them. That is the duty of the registry, and it is up to you to assess whether my attitude to that is serious, whether I have selected relevant documents, or whether those documents at first blush are irrelevant. Now, these two books at first glance are highly relevant. They are not important for the cross-examination of many Prosecution witnesses. They are, however, very important for the cross-examination of the expert witnesses, the Prosecution expert witnesses that are going to be called. They are very important for that, and they're also very important for the Defence case, for presenting evidence in the Defence case and for examining the Defence witnesses and Defence expert witnesses. Without them, you cannot view the whole. You cannot enter into the succus of the subject matter. And the books explain all my speeches and all my public appearances. It is on the basis of reading those two books that you will know in advance which testimony of which witnesses are false or not, because every witness and testimony is false which is not consistent with the ideological views that I put forward in those books and my ideology convictions are extremely nationalist in character, and I am very proud to be considered the greatest living Serb nationalist, but it is not in the primitive terms that the Prosecution is trying to prove on the basis of many false witnesses to whom answers were suggested, false answers at that. So the problem is one that can be solved if there was good-will on the part of the registry. Now, whether you're going to solve it or not is up to you to decide. So I'm not applying reprisal measures, I consider it to be completely absurd to provide you with other documents to be translated if you haven't translated the two key books.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, whilst listening to you I have just discovered another problem, a new one, and Ms. Dahl might express her view on this. You mentioned the experts who are about to come and testify and I suppose you had in mind expert Oberschall because he would really have looked into everything you have written and dissected everything. If he is to testify, you're entitled to cross-examine him of course, but as part of the equality of arms and the fair trial, you would be entitled to call your own expert in order to contradict the Prosecution's expert, and your own expert will, no doubt, support his views on this book. So under the principle of equality of arms, how could we make sure that there is this parallel attitude and the equality between the parties if this important issue which has to do with your speeches and their scope, a matter that will be used or mentioned by expert Oberschall, if you can't adduce an opposite type of evidence. So that's the problem. How does the Prosecution feel about this?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: If the question relates to the matter of translation, Mr. Seselj is confronted by the same challenge that every other accused in the Tribunal faces, which is marshalling his evidence to present his Defence case in the working languages of the Tribunal. I agree that he may wish to present his own expert testimony. We look forward to reviewing any material that he may develop in support of such testimony and we'll exercise our right to cross-examine the expert, both as to qualifications and opinions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, I suppose -- I assume, but I don't want to go into your Defence strategy, so you don't have to answer this, but I suppose this famous book, and that is 1.000 pages long that you want to have translated, is going to be something that is -- would be used by your Defence expert, if any. So what is your view on this?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Some of the experts will certainly refer to that book, but, or rather, two books will be the basis of my examination of witnesses. I have informed you that I intend to spend a lot of time when presenting my case on my examination, both the examination-in-chief carried out by legal associates and for the cross-examination. You know there's no possibility of adequately discussing the question of hate speech without those two books, and that also concerns the joint criminal enterprise because the ideology in those two books is my ideology, it's not the ideology of any of the others accused for a joint criminal enterprise. They are the inceptors of an ideology from the communists up until those who rob banks. I have to make a distinction here. I have to isolate my own view of the world, my own ideology, my own wartime objectives, and I have to make a distinction between these positions and the positions of those for whom you have said that they were my associates, but some of them are my sworn enemies, some have tried to assassinate me, eliminate me. So I have to proceed in this manner -- in fact, I don't, if you don't allow me, I don't have to do anything, but if you want a fair trial, then you have to make this possible for me. I don't know how else I should proceed. I don't have to defend myself of -- from rape, murder, the destruction of some religious site. The Prosecution doesn't allege that I was present when this was done, when such things were done; the Prosecution says that others did this while following my ideology or my speeches or other examples that I provided through my conduct, so I'm not going to be dealing with exhumations or proof of rape. But I have to deal with what I have been indicted for. As far as these two books are concerned, well I would use these two books to contradict the thesis that I was involved in a joint criminal enterprise with Veljko Kadijevic; with Blagoje Adzic, the Chief of the General Staff; with the chief of the secret police, Stanisic; the former president, Milosevic; many others. How can I refute this if you don't make it possible for me to do so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, on the 11th of October you filed a motion to reconsider my decision of the 24th of September, 2007. So technically speaking I can react to this, but the Trial Chamber that is about to be created can also answer. So please, I urge you to supplement your submissions, and there will be of course a reply from the Prosecution. Do develop your submissions and be much more specific in order to demonstrate that there are in your book paragraphs, themes, chapters that are necessary to your Defence case; otherwise, if I look at the submissions you mentioned, Mr. Krasic is the one who drafted the submission, only mentions the issue of relevance only superficially. So it might be necessary to really go to the details of it so that the Trial Chamber by way of a decision may order the registry to have the book translated, because it goes to the very foundation of your Defence case. So see this, discuss this with Mr. Krasic. I, for my part, will meet with registry services to look into the matter. I, therefore, will not make a decision right now because I feel that the Bench must take the decision. Of course the Prosecution will answer, but you can supplement your submissions by doing what you did here, by going into details, and by quoting examples. In its wisdom, the Trial Chamber, if it so feels, of course I can't speak on behalf of my fellow Judges, if it feels that the book must be translated, it may be in a position to order the book to be translated. This is all I can say right now, but once again I am telling you that nobody has any intention of preventing you from exerts your rights, and this is a good transition to move to another problem which I'm going to try and solve as well, as much as it is possible. You talked about it earlier, this is the disclosure under Rule 68, disclosure of exhibits. Last time you said, I suppose you will say the same thing today, you said that you had a Prosecution document indicating that there would be 207.000 documents that could be exculpatory documents falling under the scope of Rule 68. To see more clearly in this, Rule 68 was amended on several occasions. It was adopted on the 11th of February, 1994, revised on the 30th of January, 1995, amended on the 12th of July, 2001, amended again on the 12th of December, 2002 -- 2003, and amended again on the 28th of July, 2004. There are two relevant provisions, one (i) and (ii). And (i) says this: "The Prosecutor shall as soon as practicable disclose to the Defence any material which in the actual knowledge of the Prosecutor may suggest the innocence or mitigate the guilt of the accused or affect the credibility of Prosecution evidence." So that's very clear-cut. As to (ii), the other provision, it says this: "Without prejudice to paragraph (i), the Prosecutor shall make available to the Defence in electronic form collections of relevant material held by the Prosecutor together with appropriate computer software with which the Defence can search such collections electronically." So the Rules are very clear in this matter. Anything that is exculpatory or that is likely to have an effect on the indictment must be disclosed to you in hard copy and in your own language. That -- this arose from the latest amendment on the 28th of July, 2004. I believe that I have identified the problem. On the 30th of September, 2004, in other words, two months after the latest amendment which brought in the issue of the electronic search, the Prosecutor in charge of the case - it was then Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff - sent to Mr. Van der Spoel, who was the stand-by counsel at the time a letter, in which she said that there were seven CD-ROMs and four DVDs containing documents that could be exculpatory in nature. And this letter mentions Rule 68 without mentioning, however, (i) or (ii). That was the mistake made then by the Prosecution. This letter had been sent to your counsel, with whom you had absolutely no dealings, and it says that as far as the four DVDs were concerned, together possibly with the search engines, had to do with the 5th Military District, the 9th Knin Corps, Captain Dragan, civilian defence, General Raseta, the KOS, the Military Naval District, the Martic police, the SAO Krajina police, the Serb guards volunteers, the VRS, as well as the White Eagles. So this is what your counsel knew. As to the seven CD-ROMs, they dealt with the BH army, the Ministry of Defence, of the Interior, of the BiH, with the Green Berets, with the ZNG, with the Croatian army, with the MUP of the Croatian police, with the HOS, and with the milicija. Since then, since then, this issue was not formally solved inasmuch as you say there are 207.000 documents and you want to have them. I issued a decision several months ago inviting you specify to Ms. Dahl some key words that would enable her to search among the 207.000 documents the documents that might be under the scope of the (i) of Rule 68, and Ms. Dahl had told us that she was absolutely willing to carry out this search for you and to convey the results of it to you, provided of course you gave her some clues or key words to identify the documents. Now, what is the state of play right now as I can see -- of course I can be wrong. But on the 30th of September, 2004, officially -- it was not Ms. Dahl because she came in later, so she's not really personally responsible for this problem, but the Prosecution without really making any distinction does not make any difference between the (i) and the (ii), because if it had done so it would not have said that among the DVDs and the CD-ROMs there were exculpatory documents. Now, to date I fail to see how, but Ms. Dahl may have the key to this problem, how the Prosecution could tell you these are the documents falling under the (i) provision of Rule 68, because that would be tantamount to saying that the Prosecution would work for days, for months on end sort of reading through the 207.000 documents, would work on sorting them out, and telling you, This is an exculpatory document that may have an impact on you and may jeopardize the Prosecution case. So this is the state of play. What can we do? Because as I see things, in the coming weeks or months the Prosecution can keep trying to disclose this to you, that's one possibility; the other possibility would be that you, yourself, starting with some key words, what I had in mind, for instance, was the White Eagles or other key words, you could ask the Prosecution to give you all the documents proving that I have nothing to do with this. You could ask the Prosecution to identify for your sake the documents found in the seven CD-ROMs and the four DVDs. But failing this which is only a practical or a pragmatic measure, if you see the principle of Rule 68(i), since this matter has been in abeyance for five years, I think this is just wishful thinking. The Prosecution cannot tell you today that among the 207.000 documents there are so many which are exculpatory. Madam Dahl, do you want to supplement what I've just said in relation to this problem, which is a real problem, and I cannot deny that problem, neither can anybody else?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I first want to correct the notion that there are 207.000 documents. That's an estimate of the number of pages. The spreadsheet of the ERN -- the evidence numbers relates to 17.894 documents that result from very broad search criteria, in some cases single words or single groups represented, for instance, by the maritime military district. I want to take a step back with respect to electronic disclosure and the practice of Defence counsel. Generally, Defence counsel have asked for more rather than fewer documents in an electronic format rather than paper and in any language so that they may themselves, armed with their own knowledge of relevance and the theory of defence, investigate and explore and search the electronic collection. That modality of offering electronic collections persisted in this case until the ruling this summer that Mr. Seselj should receive material strictly within Rule 68(i) in paper and in Serbian. He may, if he wishes, print at his expense all of the documents that have been made available to him in electronic form. It is not necessary for a fair trial for the Prosecution to undertake that burden. And indeed, the material that has been disclosed to him under Rule 68(i), has been done in compliance with the ruling this summer. And as material comes within our actual knowledge, we print it, we make sure it's in a language accessible to him, and we disclose it. Now, the letter that Your Honour referred to was also offered to Mr. Seselj, and he rejected it. So we are at the eve of trial because of his deliberate unwillingness to make use of the information being made available to him and his insistence on an interpretation of the Rules and a change in the procedure that he stands alone in. So I don't have a more specific solution. The registry, as I have noted before, has offered to make printing facilities available to Mr. Seselj. We have the Excel spreadsheet of the 17.894 documents. Those are indexed by their registration numbers, and if he wishes unstructured information in paper format, which frankly I find less accessible and less useful than the electronic search terms, as a self-represented accused he is within his right to make those decisions, regardless of how unwise they may prove to be.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. You gave us some new elements, so the debate focuses on 17.894 documents and not 207.000 because it is 207.000 pages representing 17.894 documents. Mr. Seselj, Mrs. Dahl has been telling us that since the Chamber's ruling Mrs. Dahl has disclosed under Rule 68(i) all documents that are relevant, and as for the rest she's telling you to carry out the electronic search or have your associates do the electronic search in order to know exactly what is relevant, what is useful to your case. I'm sure you have another opinion as far as this is concerned, and I will now give you the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, as the Prosecutor's office is permanent, I'm not interested in the fact that Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff left, that Ms. Christine Dahl arrived, that's their problem. They're all the same to me. They're representatives of the Prosecution, and I'm trying to show that this is a political Prosecutor's office. It's a false office. Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff said that the Prosecution had identified 207.000 pages of potentially exculpatory material. When she says "identified potentially exculpatory documents," exclusively refers to Rule 68(i), exclusively. Rule 68(ii) makes no mention of identification of potentially exculpatory documents. It mentions access to collections of Prosecution material, various kinds of documents, some of which might be exculpatory but none of which have been identified as such yet. These are important distinctions to make. There's no reason for confusion. If the Prosecution identifies something as exculpatory material, well that's been identified as such forever. All the documents you mentioned as -- and the contents you mentioned, well these are important documents, even the marine section is important. They participated in land operations. JNA admirals were judged here for being involved in land operations. There was a general who was indicted for the Dubrovnik battle-field, but in many judgements rendered by the Appeals Chamber in particular, it's stated that the Prosecutor is an official acting on behalf of international justice. I can provide you with information on these judgements. As I said, an official of international justice who has two equally important duties. The Prosecutor must prosecute those, the accused of war crimes, and must also find potentially exculpatory material and provide the accused with this material in good time. You must ask the Prosecution to prove that during this five-year period the resources which they had and everything else was used to find potentially exculpatory documents in the same way that they used these resources to prosecute me and to obtain evidence against me. They have to convince you of this fact. They haven't done so, but in spite of that, they continue to violate their obligations. Ms. Hildegard Uertz-Retzlaff identified 207.000 pages, and I'm requesting that I be informed of this material because she herself stated or wrote that this was potentially exculpatory material. A new Prosecutor has arrived and says she has no idea about this, and so now I'm supposed to feel sorry for the Prosecution or the Prosecutor because the Prosecutor doesn't have time to read this. I believe that the Prosecutor has to provide me with this material even if the Prosecutor doesn't read through it because this material has been identified. And the only way I can be provided with this material is if the material is provided to me in hard copies and in the Serbian language. If they haven't done this for five years, that isn't my problem, it's their problem. If they don't hand over 207.000 pages of potentially exculpatory material, well then my basic rights as a defendant have been violated. I can't defend myself without those 207.000 pages, and I don't want those -- the number of those pages to be reduced to 206 or 205.000 pages. It's said that there are 207.000 pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Since the decision of July 7, 2007, how many documents have you disclosed as hard copy to Mr. Seselj under Rule 68(i)?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may take a minute to see if I have that information available.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am told that we have to have a break, and can you give me the answer after the break, please. We need to have a 20-minute break, and we will resume in 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, I will endeavour to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The hearing is resumed. We have but one hour. So, Mrs. Dahl, you were supposed to tell me how many documents you disclosed to Mr. Seselj under Rule 68(i).

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, we don't keep our records in that fashion. I can tell you that we have disclosed ten receipts as cover letters to anywhere between 1 and approximately 40 documents. We've put over 3.000 documents responsive to the search terms Mr. Seselj gave us at an earlier Status Conference onto the electronic disclosure system. Those are readily available today, but I'm sorry I'm not able to tell you the number of documents. We don't keep track of those kinds of statistics.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Seselj, Mrs. Dahl is telling me that she disclosed a number of documents, notably after research made, an electronic search made, out of key words that were provided by you.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can give a temporal time-period you asked me how many documents we had disclosed since this summer. So my answer was limited to disclosure after approximately June 2007.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Mr. Seselj, do you agree with what Mrs. Dahl just said?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone for Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I do not agree, Judge, because Ms. Dahl is intentionally and tendentiously leading us astray with respect to Rule 68(i) and (ii). She keeps repeating that they have enabled me some sort of search I am not interested in any search, and I would like to stop talking about those searches. Mrs. Dahl is only partially right when she said as from the summer from the Prosecution they sent me between 1 and 40 potentially exculpatory documents. Now, between 1 and 40, perhaps we could reduce that and say some 20 or maybe even less. I can't give you an exact number, but as far as I recall there certainly weren't more than 20, and one document was by Miroslav Radic, an expert defence --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: May I ask Mr. Seselj to lower his voice. I cannot hear the translation due to the volume of his voice in the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, could you please speak in a lower tone of voice, please, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, there's no sense in all this, Judge. Perhaps it would be best if I didn't say a word. Well, imagine a courtroom in the world where the accused or his Defence counsel is cautioned for speaking too loud, where does that exist? Nowhere in the world would you have a situation like that. It's only here in The Hague that this kind of thing happens to me while I was testifying as a witness in the Milosevic trial and here again during these proceedings.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, please, when we speak interpreters must translate, and sometimes it's difficult to understand when you have both the direct voice and the interpretation in the headset. Possibly we could not even hear you and just listen to the translation, but unfortunately we hear the translation and also your voice because your voice is heard in the courtroom and sometimes it's very difficult to understand what you're saying because of this. Let's go back to the issue of the documents, please.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, my voice is sometimes louder, sometimes weaker. It's usually always quite loud and strong, louder than the voices of others. I try sometimes to speak more quietly, sometimes I forget to put in the effort to speak more quietly, but if somebody's going to interrupt me all the time because of that, then what will this look like? If the problem is in the headsets, then the Prosecutor should get more high-tech headsets which will isolate all the other sounds in the courtroom except the sound coming in through the headsets. I suppose that would be a solution. But anyway, I was sent one exculpatory material from a defence expert Miroslav Radic in the trial of the Vukovar three, well, that's how the trial was colloquially known, it was otherwise Mrksic, Sljivancanin and Radic, the Prosecutor versus those three; so I hope you don't mind me calling them the Vukovar three and a number of other documents were provided me which relate to Vuk Draskovic and some others I can't enumerate them all now but certainly there weren't more than 20 documents. So the truth is somewhere halfway between the 1 and 40 mentioned by Ms. Dahl. I don't know how many there were, I didn't count them, but I did put them in some sort of order and selected some. So that is a negligible number if we compare it to the several thousand that the Prosecution has at its disposal, which the predecessor to Ms. Dahl identified as potentially exculpatory material. Now, for the Prosecution this is potentially exculpatory material as far as they're concerned and it's up to me to choose what is really relevant and what I consider to be exculpatory for me and the other documents that I can reject. But it is their duty that whenever they have an idea that something could help me in my defence and could be exculpatory to provide me with those documents. That's their obligation, but they're not fulfilling their duty or their main duty with respect to the disclosure of documents, Prosecution documents, in this case. I still haven't received all those. There are several hundred documents missing. Some they categorised as postponed disclosure documents, others they tried to serve me with exclusively in English, and others did not exist. Just the file with the number 65 ter so-and-so. Now, I wrote all this down very pedantically and sent letters to the Prosecution telling them exactly what they sent us, and I returned all the documents in English and separated all the documents that were exclusively in English, but they did not comply with their duty fully either in that regard, and I'm sure you'll remember, Judge, that you made it incumbent upon the Prosecution that together with the pre-trial proceedings of the Prosecution that I should receive the judgement in the Brdjanin trial which explains the concept of joint criminal enterprise in a novel way, but they still haven't sent me that, that's just part of the judgement. And now I am asked to respond to their pre-trial brief and you have given me a deadline which is I think the 31st of October for me to do that. So how can I do that within that deadline when they keep referring to Brdjanin and the judgement and the concept of joint criminal enterprise, whereas I don't have that and I should have it in order to be able to state my views and respond. And on a number of occasions, I have shown that they're not conscientious in performing their duty and that they're not giving me their -- what they should be, either with regard to Prosecution documents or exculpatory material or anything the Court rules. They've just started doing that yesterday ad hoc, the transcripts of testimonies of certain witnesses in other trials. Two witnesses, for example, in the Prosecutor versus Slavko Dokmanovic, that particular trial and one other witness, I forget now whether it's the Samac trial, but it doesn't matter. They've just started doing that. And they have to translate the many, many documents that they have in Serbian and provide them in hard copy. And there's only one sanction that you can apply vis-a-vis the Prosecution, and that to reject any potential Prosecution witness for whom they have not got a set of documents attached. So no witness can be brought in to testify here if he was a witness in other trials and if I haven't been provided with the transcript of the testimony of that person -- that person in Serbian. Then that person, that witness, cannot come in to give testimony here. It seems that they have had dealings with corrupt lawyers, but let me tell them, I'm not going to allow that to happen. So if I can be figurative and say that I'm going to stick to the letter of the law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, Mr. Seselj. I'm trying to move ahead regarding this very important issue, which for the moment we don't have a solution. It is true that disclosure of documents suffered from a drawback which came from the fact that this disclosure is done without the Judge's control. So when Mrs. Dahl is sending documents over to you, I have no idea what she's sending. This is what -- actually, because there's nothing in the Rules providing for this, and a great number of Judges do not want to interfere with the disclosure between parties. And because of this, sometimes you suddenly unearth problems at the very end. At the time I could have found out and I was member of Trial Chamber II and I could have found out that Mrs. Uertz-Retzlaff's letter telling you that four CDs and seven DVDs were being sent over to you and that this letter was going to create problems because at the time you did not want your stand-by lawyer Mr. Van der Spoel and he did not want to receive these CD-ROMs and DVDs. If the Judges had been aware of that at the time and had been aware of what was written in this letter I would have found out immediately that there was a problem in relation to Article 68(i). The fact that this is done outside a Judge's control does lead to these kind of problems. Secondly -- what can we say now? When you have -- when you have a lawyer - and this is not your case - but when you have a lawyer and Mrs. Dahl said this very justly earlier, the Rule provides for the lawyer -- the Prosecution to send the documents in electronic form to the lawyer, and then it's up to the counsel to try to search through these electronic documents to try and find which ones are relevant to the case as far as Article 68(i) is concerned. But the problem is that you have a right not to have a lawyer. This was a right that was recognised last year in December. Now -- and before unearthing this problem of the 207.000 pages -- problem has been unearthed belatedly but it exists now and hasn't been solved yet. Now, earlier Mrs. Dahl quoted two examples -- or one, actually, the Brdjanin case, where for the joint criminal enterprise alleged in the indictment Mr. Seselj was to have the judgement in his own language and he may believe that this comes under Rule 68(i) as far as his case is concerned. I want to note that Prosecution did not disclose the -- this appeals judgement. Then proprio motu let me mention another example. The --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You want to answer this, Mrs. Dahl?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: To facilitate the translation of relevant authorities, we filed a book of authorities that included extracts of the relevant provisions in the Brdjanin appeals judgement. I knew that it would take some time for CLSS to translate the entire judgement, but I endeavoured to make sure that that information was available to Mr. Seselj. All of the paragraphs that we cited that are either outside the Yugoslavia Tribunal's jurisdiction or are new and therefore remain to be translated, are within our book of authorities. That, I believe, is pending translation for Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine, thank you. But another example which I'm quoting. Recently a Trial Chamber made -- ruled on the Vukovar three, and so far this judgement did not recognise the existence of a joint criminal enterprise, so this judgement may be extremely interesting for the accused. Will Prosecution disclose a copy of this judgement because Vukovar is in the indictment?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: It is not our obligation to translate and disclose to Mr. Seselj the trial judgements. We prepared the book of authorities as a courtesy to help ensure a prompt starting date and to avoid translation delays associated with the entire appeals judgement. I would note that the theory in the case and the accused related to a military structure; that is different than this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me come back to Vukovar because you did not answer that. In the indictment against this accused, mention is made of Vukovar. It so happens that with regard to the Vukovar three the JCE had been invoked and the Trial Chamber decide that it was not there. So this might be -- this judgement might be relevant for this accused. Don't you think that under Rule 68(i) he should be disclosed this judgement?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, well this is the first time in my life that I have to agree with the representative of the Prosecution. The judgement as far as the Vukovar three are concerned should be sent me by the registry, not the Prosecution; but the Prosecution is duty-bound to provide me with part of the judgement from the Brdjanin trial because you issued that order. It was an official order from you that they send it to me, just like -- now, had you made the same ruling with regard to the Vukovar three, the Prosecution would have had to do so, too, but in this case it's not the duty of the Prosecution but the registry. And I need both judgements. Because if no joint criminal enterprise existed in Vukovar, how come I'm there? When Vukovar was liberated I happened to be in Knin which is several hundred kilometres away from Vukovar. So if there's no joint criminal enterprise, there's nothing over there, as far as I'm concerned, of course. So that judgement is absolutely necessary. You're either going to issue an order to the registry to provide me with the document or the Prosecution, but otherwise it's not the duty of the Prosecution to do so unless you specifically order it to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We're going to move to private session for a few seconds because I want to tackle an issue.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're back in open session, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Well, I'm hoping to get some news. Last time I'd asked you to sort of get together, hoping that if there was a meeting it might make it possible to reach an agreement as to certain crimes and this would curtail the need for the calling of specific witnesses. The fact that these crimes happened does not involve your own liability in any direct way because you pleaded guilty and you negate any connection or deny any connection between the authors -- the perpetrators of the crime and yourself. So I made an order and I thought that the OTP was in favour of such a meeting. Has any progress been made, Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no meeting took place. I expressed my readiness to meet on condition that my legal advisors, case manager, and five basic investigators also take part, so I'm ready to have that contact. I'm ready to have the contact last several days and to present certain documents which testify to the unfounded character of parts of the indictment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] What about you, Ms. Dahl? So Mr. Seselj was in favour of a meeting provided his advisors were present as well as his case manager.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: The record of the prior Status Conference differs as to what Mr. Seselj said. I asked for him to provide me with a letter about the topics he was willing to discuss and whom he would wish in attendance by name. He said he would never send such a letter and the matter ended there. He is at a distinct disadvantage being unrepresented. He would be required to have the formalities provided for in the Rules regarding warnings and the making of an official record of the interview. If there are places where Mr. Seselj, having been duly warned, is willing to make statements, we will certainly receive that information from him, but we will use what he says against him to secure a conviction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Madam Dahl -- Ms. Dahl, is saying two things: You were to send her a letter stating the points to be discussed with her; secondly, she's telling you that if ever there was such a meeting, it would be recorded, and since it is important and that what you may say during that meeting with the Prosecution, may be recorded. And she added that it could be possibly held against you. What do you have to say?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I assume that you're fully conscious that the interpretation of Ms. Dahl is not truthful. You issued a ruling after the Status Conference, and at the Status Conference I said that I was ready to talk, that I was ready to have a meeting with the representatives of the Prosecution, but I did not express the wish for that. I have no wishes in that regard. I never want to see in my life representatives of this Prosecution. I have no wish to see them at all, but I do have the readiness to do so. I am ready to talk in order to rationalise resources, in order to convince the Prosecution how -- what failures they have in their department and to give up on certain parts of the indictment which would make this trial simpler. And so when I show them the documents that I had nothing to do with crimes in Herzegovina, for instance, and the people who were accused of the crimes over there have nothing to do with me, if I show them that I have nothing to do with ascribed crimes in Sarajevo, in Zvornik, in Vukovar, if I were to show them in Vojvodina there was no attack on the civilian population let alone a systematic and widespread ones, then they could give up on the whole indictment, of course had there not been a political motive to raise the indictment in the first place and that western powers didn't stand behind the indictment for their own interests. So I'm ready to do that, but I'm not asking and have no wish or desire to see them. I have certain conditions, and it was my condition that the whole encounter be taped by video-camera, that was my condition expressed at the Status Conference. If you will recall, and it was only under those conditions that I was ready to discuss anything with them, that everything is taped and recorded and that my legal advisors, legal associates, are there of course, the investigators to be paid their per diems and costs for coming here, otherwise I have nothing that I need to write to the Prosecution in that regard. The initiative is up to them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I can see that, in fact, you are very close to one another since you asked the meeting to be recorded; Ms. Dahl wanted that, too. So there is an agreement. The only problem is the issue of your advisors, your associates, who are now in Belgrade. If they were to come, of course their trip must be paid for and they must have an allowance. That's part of the decision on financing the Defence. Third point, I can't remember, but Ms. Dahl might be quite right on this. At the latest Status Conference you would have said that you needed to know what the meeting was going to be about, and if she knew the items she could organize such a meeting as long as she had the topics. And apparently she was expecting you to send her a letter listing the various items. Well, you've numbered them. You spoke about Vojvodina, about Sarajevo, Zvornik, et cetera, so there are a number of items, but it may be that a letter would have made it possible for Ms. Dahl to organize the meeting. Well, I did what I could so that the parties, Prosecution and the Defence, agree on facts or on issues of law. Should there be an agreement, you could notify this to the Trial Chamber. I had also told you that it was really important for both parties to have this type of meeting. I told you that experience shows me that 80 per cent of trial time is devoted to crime base facts and 20 per cent to the real issues, namely, the liability or not. And I thought that it was better to spend most of the time on the issues related to liability if one could have an agreement on the facts that there was looting or destruction, anything that is unfortunately intrinsic to any conflict. And I wanted the trial to be useful, most of the time being devoted to the issues of liability. This is the reason why I issued the order. It's not too late for you to meet. It's up to you to make a move. I've done as much as I could in this matter. There's another 30 minutes left -- yes, Ms. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I had two matters of housekeeping that I thought should be raised.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Mr. Seselj submitted number 328, a consolidated version of his special defence, and I note that at the last two pages, 9 and 10 of the translation, he indicates that he has submitted it to the Trial Chamber and within our two paragraphs with requests for relief or judicial action. The matter itself, the submission, has not been filed to cause it to be a motion before the Trial Chamber. It was actually just served on the Prosecution. So I would think that the Registrar needs to file it and present it as an item for judicial action before the Chamber. That's number 328. Second, with regard to the second amended indictment, the Chamber will recall its decision of 14 September. There were issues left for the Prosecution to take action upon, and on 28 September we filed a notice of compliance. There were four questions that needed resolution concerning several paragraphs. We had proposed in paragraph 4 a time-frame for the accused's leadership of the Serbian Chetnik Movement in response to the decision at paragraph 22. At paragraph 7 of the indictment we included an enumeration of the crimes that were a foreseeable consequence of the accused's attempt to permanently expel Muslims and Croats in order to create a state dominated by Serbs, which he refers to as Greater Serbia. Paragraph 14 is -- represents the Prosecution's redaction of language rejected by the Chamber in paragraph 33 of the decision concerning the Prosecution's allegations regarding intent and awareness of risk. Finally, paragraph 34 of the indictment presents the proposed resolution of the allegations concerning plunder that were put to the Prosecution in the decision of 14 September. I bring this to the attention of the Chamber because we've asked for an order to be entered, directing the registry to file the second amended indictment, and we will supply the corresponding annexes. I want to just tidy up the housekeeping because the decision left open several questions and the Prosecution has made its choices consequent upon the decision. Then that requires Chamber's approval.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. We shall issue an order on the amendments that you made following our decision of 14th September, 2007. So there is a one half-hour left. Yes, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I would first like to respond to what Ms. Dahl has said. My consolidated submission on special defence was forwarded to the Trial Chamber and to the Prosecution and were also provided to the registry, and it was for the registry to make copies and to provide the Chamber with a copy and the Prosecution with a copy, not just the Prosecution. According to the rules on special defence, submissions are only provided to the Prosecution, not to the Trial Chamber. On this occasion, I forwarded a copy to the Trial Chamber, as I believed it was essential for you to be familiar with it, as we're dealing with your order to have such submission filed. Then secondly, Ms. Dahl also commented on certain other things which shows she knows nothing about the concept, the idea, of Greater Serbia. If she read through my two books, "The Ideology of Serbian Nationalism" and "The Roman Catholic Project of an Artificial Greater State," well everything would be clear to her and she would abandon her pursuit of such an indictment because I never pursued policies according to which Serbs, Catholics, and Serb Muslims, were to be expelled from the territory of the imagined Greater Serbia. I was interested in awakening the national consciousness of Serbs who were Catholics and of Muslims who were -- and of Serbs who were Muslims, since these people had been put outside or expelled from their maternal nation. So with your leave, Judge, before we conclude, I have three other issues I would like to raise. The first issue concerns a problem created by the Prosecution recently. They exerted -- by exerting pressure on potential Defence witnesses and by requesting that they come for another meeting with the Prosecution. We're talking about people whom the Prosecution interviewed several years ago. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: We need to go into closed session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're giving names again. Yes, you're giving names again.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I apologise. It's not necessary to move into private session. These are names of Prosecution witnesses. These are potential Defence witnesses --

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And their names are mentioned in my criminal file -- criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One moment, Ms. Dahl. Here's the problem, Mr. Seselj gave a few names and I have time to issue a redacting order because we have a time lag of 30 minutes. He's mentioned three names because he says they are Defence witnesses so I am entitled to give the names. And you? What do you say? Are they your witnesses?

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, it would be inappropriate for me to discuss protected witnesses or to acknowledge whether or not witnesses who are protected are, in fact, people who Mr. Seselj has identified. We have been through this problem before. I'm not going to play the game with him when he puts out a game and sees whether we react. This is a neutral rule designed to protect all witnesses from his attempt to ferret out protective measures.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, Ms. Dahl is right. I'm going to explain to you why. She has her witnesses and you may not know some of them because the obligation to disclose their names to you comes 30 days before commencement of trial. You have your own witnesses, they may be the same, we don't know, and the very fact that you would give a name might, might, indeed, harm the protective measures because it could be that one of the witnesses has been granted already a pseudonym and protective measures. So please, don't state any names. Just say Mr. X, Mr. Y, or Mr. Z, that would be much more simple. I'm going to issue a redacting order for the three names to be redacted because they could be protected witnesses, and I cannot risk disclosing names, but just give any names by saying X, Y, Z. That's no problem. Go ahead, Mr. Seselj.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I object to such position, to your position. I mentioned the names of potential Defence witnesses. I also mentioned their names in the criminal report I filed. Any time I mention the names of potential Defence witnesses, Ms. Dahl can't get up on her feet and ask for the transcript to be redacted because she assumes that perhaps we're also dealing with witnesses of their own.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I agree with you. You are entitled to state names of potential Defence witnesses. I fully agree with you, I fully agree, but, Mr. Seselj, a situation may arise where, without you knowing it, the names you give of potential witnesses are the names of Prosecution witnesses who have already been granted protective measures without you even being aware of it. That's the problem, you see. We don't want to prevent you from stating names. It's just that we might find ourselves in a situation where you might state your intent to call 10, 20, 30, 40, or 50 witnesses, among whom we might have people who are already Prosecution witnesses without you knowing it. Do you understand the problem?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't, Judge. Your interpretation is quite unacceptable because when I mention a name -- well, it seems as if I can't mention a single name because it's possible that a Prosecution witness might be at stake, someone whose name hasn't been disclosed. In the course of my case, I'll be mentioning a number of names.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You know what must have happened in practical terms, the Prosecutor, the investigator, went to collect testimonies. They met with people, and witnesses probably made statements. You, yourself, through your associates, you went there and you met with individuals, with witnesses, and it may be that some of them had already been contacted by the OTP. And these individuals may have already given statements. There may be situations in which these individuals had not told you that they had already given statements, and you in good faith - and I fully agree with everything you said - you were -- went out to search for witnesses and you tell me, I've got this one, that one, and the other. Fine. But these people, Mr. X, Mr. Y, Mr. Z, I don't know whether these people will apply for protective measures. I don't know yet. Secondly, these people whose names you mention, they may have been granted protective measures already once. You don't know about it.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Don't allow Ms. Dahl to interrupt me now. I want to tell you about this and then you can redact the entire transcript after that.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I may propose briefly if Mr. Seselj needs to discuss specific names of individuals, we can of course always go into closed session. There's nothing to prevent him identifying people and discussing them; it's only a question of whether it's public and whether he makes the speech in public about it as opposed to a presentation in closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, my concern, Mr. Seselj, is to make sure some witnesses are protected, whether they are Defence or Prosecution witnesses. So whenever you want to mention names, I'd rather we move to private session, even the confidentiality were to be lifted later, if the name you mention is not at all relevant as far as protective measures are concerned. So, Mr. Registrar, let's move to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We only have 13 minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We're in open session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You have the floor.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- We could be dealing with a protected witness for the Prosecution --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We had no interpretation because of a mix-up in channels.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't understand this. It's intolerable. It's tolerable that I can't mention anyone's name in open session, not even the name of the Pope, because anyone in the world could be a potential Prosecution witness with protective measures, but I must be allowed to mention all names unless the Prosecution has informed me in good time that such and such a person is a protected witness. I can't mention the name of a single family member either. I can't mention the names of my friends, of my legal associates. Perhaps they are also protected Prosecution witnesses. I can mention anyone's name unless the Prosecution has informed me of the fact that such and such a person is a protected witness. And there's one other thing, I can do it when I know that someone is a protected witness and will be testifying against me in a month or two, but a prior Prosecution witness appears in open session, I have the right to ask that witness about the behaviour of this other person without mentioning that he's a protected witness against me because I know that his conduct was of a certain kind. Judge, I don't understand what's happening here. I can mention anyone's name without saying that it's a protected witness. I may even mention the name of a protected witness, but I must not reveal the witness's role. I can mention the witness in another context. I can say such and such a person threatened me, such and such a person threw a stone at me. I can mention the person's name, even though he might be a Prosecution's witness, a protected witness. But unless I say such and such a person is a Prosecution's witness and is protected, I haven't violated the Rules. It is elementary. If you don't allow me to mention anyone's name or if every time I mention a name we have to move into closed session, well these proceedings are just nonsensical, then I just won't defend myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just one thing, Mr. Seselj. You know that we have this 30-day rule. So as of December 4th we'll have the first witness, which means on November 4th, just a few days from now, you will get the list of protected witnesses. And then all those who are not on the list, you'll be able to mention them. If your own investigators have determined -- have found witnesses in the field in your cross-examination you can say, Sir, you said this and Mr. X is saying exactly the opposite. Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour, respectfully I disagree with the interpretation and advice you're giving to Mr. Seselj of what would be appropriate once he is giving the list of protected witness. First I want to make clear that some witnesses have delayed disclosure consequent on the date of their testimony rather than the commencement of the presentation of evidence. Second, many witnesses because of the victimisation that they have suffered are to be referred to solely by their pseudonym and in an abundance of caution given the nature of the allegations against Mr. Seselj that we tread very carefully and precisely upon what is considered appropriate when identifying people in session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, you're absolutely right. We have another category of witnesses. We have witnesses whose names will be disclosed to you just 30 days before they testify. So we could have a witness scheduled for March and you will be told the name of this person in February. This is what the Rule provides for, Rule 75. And then of course you may not know that these people are protected, and if you reveal their name by accident and if Prosecution notes that this is a person for which she has asked protective measures and non-disclosure 30 days, she will ask for a redaction of the name or she will not, she may not. But this is the rule and this is what is provided for in the Rules. So she is right, but you are also right because to the extent that you may mention names of witnesses, that even though you may not know yourself that they are protected witnesses to which protective measures were granted. So it is very complicated. I fully understand that and I'm trying to convey this to you. As far as possible, try not to mention any names. If you want to mention a name, well ask for private session just for a few seconds. Just tell us, I want to talk about Mrs. X, is there a problem? If Prosecution said, There's no problem, you can mention her name, you can say Mrs. X in open session. If there is a problem, you will say just X without giving the name. This is how it should work, Mr. Seselj. But your approach is partly right but Mrs. Dahl is also right. There are Prosecution witnesses that have requested protective measures to be granted, and it's up to her to make sure that this is done. And as Judge, I have to make sure that these witnesses are safe. You had two other topics to mention, so please hurry because we only have five minutes left.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Judge, I'm very grateful to you for having explained to me the fact that I won't have a defence of any kind. You've done it very clearly and it doesn't make sense for me to say anything now if I can't mention a single name because perhaps one fears that that individual is a protected Prosecution witness, and if I can't mention the names of potential Defence witnesses either because some will request protective measures, well not a single Defence witness will ask for protective measures. They'll be proud to testify for the Defence here, and only criminals will ask for protective measures because they won't have physical threats, they'll only have the danger of being designated as disrespectful individuals in Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I have to object to this persistent attempt to impugn the integrity of witnesses who appear before the Tribunal. I have to say that there is no such thing as a Defence witness or a Prosecution witness; this is a search for truth and justice. These are witnesses of the Tribunal. It is wrong to brand people who come before this Tribunal as criminals or cowards. To vilify these people publicly is part of Mr. Seselj's campaign against the Tribunal and it needs to stop here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Seselj, when a witness comes, the witness will take the oath, make the solemn declaration saying he will tell the truth. If he's lying, he could be prosecuted for contempt, so he's under oath. And during your cross-examination you're entitled to test and challenge the credibility of this witness. You may even try and corner him to saying that he is doing a perjury, but that's your right, you're entitled to that. But out front, you know, before these people take the oath you cannot say anything about them, saying that they're going to lie or maybe you believe that they're going to lie, but we don't know it and it's up to the Trial Chamber to decide what -- how credible a witness is. If the witness does a false testimony, the witness will be prosecuted and this has already been done here. So we're not trying to prevent you from defending yourself. You know that very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But we have protective measures that are in place -- Mrs. Dahl.

utterances.speaker: MS. DAHL
utterances.text: I'm sorry, but it's worse than that. Mr. Seselj uses this Status Conference to send a message to people who are preparing to come and tell the truth before this Tribunal that they will be branded traitors, that they will be branded liars, that frightens people and it is wrong to send that message out of this courtroom in an attempt to dissuade people from coming before this Tribunal under oath to tell the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Mr. Seselj, what can you answer?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, it would be best to declare that the proceeding is secret, you should prevent me from attending it, and you can just send me a judgement by post. And everything you have said, Judge, and especially what Ms. Dahl has said, leads me to draw that -- draw that conclusion. You can have a secret proceedings, you can forbid me from attending the proceedings, and send me a judgement, whatever it may be, by post. There's no other way to proceed because what you are doing here today is scandalous. I have the right to tell any witness that he is lying and that his testimony is false. I have that right. And when cross-examining that -- such witnesses, I'll use the same means that the Prosecution uses when cross-examining Defence witnesses in all cases, I'll use all those means. I know very well what Geoffrey Nice did with Defence witnesses in the Milosevic case. I know, I know everything by heart, and I will demonstrate that here in the courtroom. But presenting these false witnesses, you won't succeed in that. All the Prosecution witnesses are false witnesses, that's the main thesis of my case. No one will prevent me from saying that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Nobody is challenging your right, your right to say that these are false witnesses, nobody is challenging that. However, that is what Mrs. Dahl said very justly, some people are coming to testify. If you are going to say out front that Mr X or Y are false witnesses, they will not come here to tell the truth. They will be prevented from that. Mrs. Dahl and you both want people to come here to tell the truth. If Mrs. Dahl was saying exactly -- doing exactly the same things, saying Mr. Seselj's witnesses are false witnesses, you would be the first one to protest, and justly so. So we will have witnesses coming. We do not know whether they'll be telling the truth. They will take the oath. You will do your cross, Judges will ask questions. Mrs. Dahl will ask her own questions during the direct examination. This is how it will happen. I now have to stop here. It's quarter to 2.00. There's another trial starting this afternoon. There are questions pending, and they may be mentioned during the Pre-Trial Conference held on Tuesday, November 6, and we will then have the opportunity of meeting again. Thank you all.
